assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Count the pieces of evidence in this debate. How many studies did Dr. Lune present? How many did Cask actually address? What happened to the ones he skipped?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Nice. Now, how would you distinguish Occam's Broom from Occam's Razor? Both involve removing something to make an argument cleaner. What is the critical difference?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Alderman Cask is polished, confident, and practiced at public persuasion. He is not stupid — he knows exactly what he is doing. He speaks with authority and eye contact, making the audience feel that he is the reasonable one in the room.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Cask smiles at you as you enter the guildhall. 'Ah, another concerned citizen. Good. You'll want to hear both sides of this water business. I think you'll find the evidence is quite reassuring — once you look at all of it.' He emphasizes 'all' while presenting only his half.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the broom, Dr. Lune is able to re-present the ignored studies to the crowd. Cask is forced to address them directly and his position weakens visibly. The guildhall votes to commission an independent review. Cask, cornered, mutters about 'activist science' but loses the room.

source.source_material: Dennett's Intuition Pumps Ch. 2 (Occam's Broom) + PHIL 201 lecture notes

scenario.context: The player enters the Artisan Quarter of Greyhold, where the Painters' Guild has strict rules: all murals must use the traditional five-colour palette, depict historical scenes, and follow the guild's compositional grid. A young painter named Cael has been expelled for breaking every rule. But his work is extraordinary — and the crowds love it. The guild master, Torvin, is furious. The player is asked to mediate.
scenario.text: Torvin crosses his arms. 'Rules exist for a reason. Cael thinks he can just ignore centuries of tradition. Any fool can splash paint on a wall and call it art. Discipline is what separates craft from chaos.' Cael shakes his head. 'I didn't ignore the rules, Torvin. I studied them for six years. I can paint a perfect guild mural in my sleep. I broke the grid because I understood exactly what it was doing and what it was preventing. I used a seventh colour because I know why the palette was limited to five and what opens up when you add two more. You can't jump out of a system you don't understand — you just flail. I understood the system, and then I jumped.'
scenario.speaker_context: Cael is demonstrating 'jootsing' — Jumping Out Of The System. Dennett borrowed this term from Douglas Hofstadter. The key insight is that creative rule-breaking requires deep knowledge of the rules being broken. Cael is not an ignorant rebel; he is a master who chose to transcend the system from a position of understanding.

structure.pattern_description: Dennett argues that genuine creativity requires first mastering the rules of the system you are working in, and then deliberately violating specific rules for specific reasons. Random rule-breaking is just noise. Informed rule-breaking — knowing which rule to break, why, and what it will produce — is jootsing. Cael exemplifies this: he mastered the guild system completely before choosing which constraints to violate and why.
structure.formal_form: System S has rules {R1, R2, ...Rn}. Agent masters S fully. Agent identifies that Ri constrains possibility space in a specific way. Agent deliberately violates Ri to achieve effect E that is impossible within S. This is jootsing. Contrast: Agent who does not understand S violates rules randomly — this is not jootsing, it is noise.
structure.why_right: Jootsing is valuable because it distinguishes productive creativity from mere rebellion. It explains why the most innovative artists, scientists, and thinkers are typically those who first achieved deep mastery of their traditions. You must understand the walls before you can know which one to knock down and what lies beyond it.
structure.counterpoint: Not all rule-breaking requires full mastery. Sometimes outsiders see possibilities that insiders cannot because insiders are too embedded in the system. Jootsing privileges insider creativity, but naive outsider perspectives occasionally produce genuine breakthroughs too.

assessment.identification_prompt: Torvin says Cael is just ignoring the rules. Cael says something different. What is Cael's actual claim about his relationship to the guild's rules, and why does it matter?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Torvin that Cael is just a rule-breaker and rules should be followed.
Player sides with Cael but frames it as 'rules are meant to be broken' — generic rebellion without understanding the deeper point.
Player recognizes that Cael learned the rules before breaking them and that this matters, but cannot articulate why the distinction between informed and uninformed rule-breaking is important.
Player identifies the key insight: creative rule-breaking requires mastery of the system being transcended. Cael's innovation is grounded in understanding, not ignorance.

Player articulates the jootsing principle, explains the mastery-then-transcendence structure, can give an example from another domain (e.g., jazz musicians who master theory before improvising), and considers whether outsider creativity is a counterexample or a different phenomenon.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine two people break the same rule. One has never heard of the rule and breaks it by accident. The other studied the rule for years and breaks it on purpose for a specific reason. Is their rule-breaking the same? Why or why not?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the harder question. Can you think of a case where someone who did not understand the system at all produced something genuinely creative by breaking its rules? If so, does that refute jootsing, or is something else going on?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cael is intense, articulate, and slightly arrogant — the arrogance of someone who has done the work and knows it. Torvin is rigid, proud of tradition, and genuinely believes the rules protect quality. Neither is a villain.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Cael is painting when you approach. Without looking up: 'They'll tell you I'm a rebel. Ask them if any rebel in history first spent six years perfecting what they were rebelling against. Then ask why that might matter.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player articulates the jootsing principle, Torvin grudgingly admits that Cael's mastery is genuine but insists the guild needs some rules. This opens a negotiation: which rules are load-bearing and which are mere tradition? The player helps draft a new guild charter that distinguishes structural principles from arbitrary conventions.

source.source_material: Dennett's Intuition Pumps Ch. 2 (Jootsing, from Hofstadter) + PHIL 201 lecture notes

scenario.context: The player visits a wandering sage named Brother Aelm who has set up a small shrine in the market square. He offers 'wisdom' to passersby in exchange for donations. A young apprentice named Kira has been attending his talks and is deeply impressed. She urges the player to listen.
scenario.text: Brother Aelm closes his eyes and intones: 'Love is just a word.' Kira gasps softly. Aelm continues: 'Think on it, friends. We chase love, we kill for love, we die for love — and yet in the end, it is just a word. Four letters. A breath of air. Everything we build on it is built on nothing more than a sound.' Several listeners nod sagely. Kira whispers to you: 'Isn't that profound?'
scenario.speaker_context: Brother Aelm has uttered what Dennett calls a 'deepity' — a statement that is ambiguous between two readings. On one reading (love is literally a word in the English language), it is trivially true but not profound. On the other reading (the thing we call love is nothing more than a linguistic construct with no real substance), it would be profound if true — but it is false. The statement gets its rhetorical power by sliding between the two readings.

structure.pattern_description: A deepity is a statement that seems profound but achieves this effect through ambiguity. It has two readings: (1) a trivially true reading that is not interesting, and (2) a reading that would be profound if true but is false or unsupported. The listener experiences the truth of reading 1 and the depth of reading 2 simultaneously, creating an illusion of profound truth. 'Love is just a word' is trivially true (love is a word in English) and profoundly false (the emotion, the bond, the experience of love is not reducible to its linguistic label).
structure.formal_form: Statement S has reading R1 (trivially true, not profound) and reading R2 (profound if true, but false or unsupported). S appears profound because the listener unconsciously blends the certainty of R1 with the significance of R2.
structure.why_wrong: Deepities are intellectually dishonest because they exploit ambiguity to simulate profundity. They create the feeling of insight without delivering any actual content. Once you separate the two readings, the magic disappears: one reading is boring and the other is wrong.
structure.counterpoint: Not every ambiguous statement is a deepity. Some genuinely profound statements resist easy paraphrase because the subject matter is genuinely complex. The test for a deepity is whether separating the readings collapses the profundity — if each reading on its own is either trivial or false, it is a deepity.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kira thinks Brother Aelm said something profound. Did he? What exactly does 'Love is just a word' mean, and is it as deep as it sounds?

rubric.description: Player agrees the statement is profound or cannot identify any problem.
Player feels the statement is empty but cannot explain why.
Player identifies that the statement is ambiguous or vague but does not clearly separate the two readings.
Player separates the trivially true reading (love is a word in English) from the would-be-profound reading (love is nothing but a word) and shows that the profundity collapses.
Player identifies the deepity structure, separates both readings, explains the mechanism of false profundity through ambiguity, and can generate another example of a deepity.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Try completing the sentence two ways. First: 'Love is just a word — it appears in the dictionary between lord and low.' True? Sure, but so what. Now try: 'Love is just a word — so the feeling you have for your family is nothing real.' True? That seems obviously wrong. Which reading was making you feel like it was profound?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Can you think of another statement that works the same way? Hint: 'God is love' and 'Everything happens for a reason' are commonly cited candidates. Try to separate their readings.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Brother Aelm is serene, soft-spoken, and practiced at sounding wise. He is not a fraud exactly — he half-believes his own pronouncements. He has never had anyone actually unpack one of his sayings before. Kira is earnest and impressionable, eager to find meaning.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Aelm opens one eye as you approach. 'You look like someone searching for something, traveller. Let me offer you this: we are all stories telling ourselves.' He pauses meaningfully. Kira nudges you: 'See? He just does that.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player unpacks the deepity, Kira has an aha moment: 'Wait — so it sounds deep because I'm hearing two things at once?' Aelm, flustered, tries another deepity. The player can debunk a series of them, and Kira learns to do it herself, unlocking her as a recurring ally who flags rhetorical tricks in future encounters.

source.source_material: Dennett's Intuition Pumps Ch. 2 (Deepities) + PHIL 201 lecture notes

scenario.context: The player sits in on a debate at the Scholars' Hall between two philosophers. Professor Venn is arguing that animals cannot truly suffer because they lack self-awareness. His opponent, Dr. Calloway, has been pressing him with examples of animal pain behaviour. Venn is getting cornered.
scenario.text: Professor Venn straightens his spectacles. 'Dr. Calloway has shown us some interesting examples of animal behaviour. But surely the capacity for genuine suffering requires self-reflection — the ability to think about one's own pain, to know that one is in pain. Surely a creature that cannot contemplate its own existence cannot be said to truly suffer. And surely we can all agree that self-reflection requires language, which animals lack.' He leans back as if the case is settled.
scenario.speaker_context: Professor Venn has used 'surely' three times in quick succession, each time to pass off a highly contestable philosophical claim as though it were obvious common sense. None of these claims are self-evident: whether suffering requires self-reflection, whether animals lack self-reflection, and whether self-reflection requires language are all active debates in philosophy of mind.

structure.pattern_description: Dennett identifies 'surely' as a rhetorical operator that attempts to sneak a controversial claim past the audience by presenting it as something everyone already agrees with. When a speaker says 'surely X,' they are signalling that X does not need argument — it is supposed to be obvious. But in philosophy and critical thinking, the claims most worth examining are often the ones preceded by 'surely.' If it really were obvious, you would not need the word.
structure.formal_form: Claim C is controversial or unsupported. Speaker prefixes C with 'surely,' converting it rhetorically from 'I assert C (and here is my argument)' to 'We all already know C (so no argument is needed).' This bypasses the burden of proof.
structure.why_wrong: The 'surely' operator substitutes rhetorical confidence for actual argument. Each of Venn's three 'surely' claims is a substantive philosophical thesis that requires defence. By prefacing them with 'surely,' he avoids providing that defence while creating the impression that the debate is already settled.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes 'surely' is used legitimately to flag genuine common ground. 'Surely 2+2=4' is not smuggling a controversial claim. The red flag is when 'surely' precedes a claim that reasonable people actually disagree about — that is when it functions as a thinking shortcut rather than an honest appeal to shared knowledge.

assessment.identification_prompt: Professor Venn used the word 'surely' three times. What work is that word doing in his argument? Is it helping or hiding something?

rubric.description: Player does not notice anything wrong or finds Venn's argument convincing.
Player feels Venn is being too confident but cannot pinpoint the mechanism.
Player notices the repeated 'surely' and senses it is covering for weak points, but cannot explain the rhetorical function.
Player identifies that 'surely' is doing the work of argument without actually being an argument — it presents contestable claims as obvious to bypass the burden of proof.

Player identifies the 'surely' operator, explains that each 'surely' flags a claim that actually needs defence, can list the three specific contestable claims Venn smuggled through, and notes when 'surely' is legitimate versus when it is a red flag.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Try an experiment. Remove the word 'surely' from each of Venn's sentences and read them again as bare claims. Do they still sound obviously true? Or do they suddenly sound like things you might want to argue about?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now, Dennett suggests a reading trick: whenever you encounter 'surely' in a philosophical text, replace it with 'I don't have an argument for this but I really want you to believe it.' Does that change how you read Venn's speech? Can you think of a case where 'surely' is used honestly?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Professor Venn is distinguished, silver-haired, and accustomed to deference. He uses 'surely' like a verbal gavel — to close discussion rather than open it. He is not dishonest, just so steeped in his own assumptions that he has stopped questioning them.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Venn peers at you over his spectacles. 'Surely you, as an educated person, can see the distinction between a dog yelping and a human being suffering. They are categorically different things. Surely.' He says the last 'surely' with a slight smile, as if daring you to disagree with the obvious.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the 'surely' operator, Dr. Calloway jumps in: 'Yes! That is exactly the move. Every time he says surely, mark it — that is where the real argument should be.' Venn sputters. The player earns a thinking-tool card: 'The Surely Alarm — when you hear surely, check whether an argument is hiding behind it.'

source.source_material: Dennett's Intuition Pumps Ch. 2 (The 'surely' operator) + PHIL 201 lecture notes

scenario.context: The player joins a strategy meeting in a besieged fort. The commander, Captain Rhea, must decide whether to hold position or attempt a breakout through the eastern valley. Her three advisors have been debating for hours, each hedging their recommendations with so many caveats that nothing actionable has emerged. Scout Pella, the youngest, has been silent.
scenario.text: Advisor Brant strokes his beard: 'The eastern valley might be passable, depending on conditions, though of course we cannot know for certain, and there are risks either way, so perhaps we should gather more intelligence before committing to anything definitive.' Advisor Maren nods: 'I would tend to agree that there are arguments on both sides, and a prudent course would be to weigh the options further.' Captain Rhea turns to Pella. Pella stands. 'The valley is passable. I ran it last night. There are forty soldiers at the narrows, not the two hundred Brant estimated. If we go at dawn with the full company, we break through. If we wait, they reinforce and we starve. I stake my rank on it.' The room goes quiet.
scenario.speaker_context: Pella demonstrates what Dennett calls 'goulding' — named after the paleontologist Stephen Jay Gould, who was willing to advance bold, specific, falsifiable claims and stake his reputation on them. Pella has done the reconnaissance, reached a specific conclusion, and committed to it publicly. The advisors, by contrast, are hedging to the point of uselessness.

structure.pattern_description: Dennett uses 'goulding' to describe the intellectual virtue of making bold, specific, testable claims rather than retreating into safe, unfalsifiable hedging. Pella's claim is specific (forty soldiers), testable (you can verify by scouting), and she has staked her credibility on it. The advisors' positions are so hedged that they cannot be wrong — but they also cannot guide action. Goulding is intellectually courageous: it risks being refuted, but that is exactly what makes it useful.
structure.formal_form: Agent A faces uncertainty. Rather than hedging with 'it might be X, or possibly Y, depending on factors,' A commits to a specific claim C that is falsifiable and actionable. A accepts the reputational cost if C turns out wrong. This is goulding: intellectual courage in the form of specificity.
structure.why_right: Hedging endlessly is safe for the hedger but useless for decision-making. A specific, falsifiable claim can be tested, acted on, and corrected. Knowledge advances through bold conjectures and refutations, not through covering all bases so thoroughly that nothing is actually said. Pella's claim could be wrong — but if it is, they will know quickly and can adapt. The advisors' hedging gives them nothing to adapt from.
structure.counterpoint: Goulding can become recklessness if the bold claim is not grounded in evidence. Pella's boldness is warranted because she actually scouted the valley. Boldness without homework is not goulding — it is bluffing. The virtue is in the combination of specificity and groundedness.

assessment.identification_prompt: The advisors and Pella are both trying to help Captain Rhea. But their approaches are very different. What is the difference, and which is more useful? Is there a risk to Pella's approach?

rubric.description: Player sees no meaningful difference between the approaches or prefers the advisors' caution.
Player prefers Pella's directness but frames it as personality ('she's brave') rather than an epistemic virtue.
Player identifies that Pella's claim is specific and actionable while the advisors' hedging is not, but does not connect this to the broader principle of falsifiability or intellectual courage.

Player articulates that Pella's boldness is an epistemic virtue: specific claims can be tested and corrected, while maximally hedged positions are unfalsifiable and therefore useless for guiding action.

Player explains goulding as a thinking tool, distinguishes it from recklessness (Pella did the reconnaissance), connects it to falsifiability, and can identify conditions where caution is appropriate versus where it becomes paralytic hedging.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine you are Captain Rhea. Advisor Brant has told you 'it might be passable, depending on conditions.' What can you do with that information? Now Pella has told you 'forty soldiers, dawn, full company.' What can you do with that? Which one actually helps you decide?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now the hard question: when is hedging the right move? Is there a version of the advisors' caution that would be genuinely valuable rather than paralytic? What distinguishes honest uncertainty from cowardly hedging?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pella is young, direct, and slightly impatient with indecision. She respects the advisors but has learned that over-caution can be as dangerous as recklessness. Captain Rhea is a careful leader who values both courage and evidence. Brant and Maren are experienced but have become so risk-averse that they have forgotten the cost of inaction.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Pella is checking her boots by the fire when you approach. 'You want to know why I spoke up? Because another hour of maybe-this-maybe-that and we all starve. I ran the valley. I counted the soldiers. If I'm wrong, I'll own it. When's the last time Brant owned anything?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player endorses goulding, Captain Rhea greenlights the dawn breakout. Pella's intelligence proves accurate and the company breaks through. If the player asks about the risk, Rhea nods: 'Risk is the price of specificity. But at least we know what we're risking.' Post-battle, Pella offers a follow-up: 'Now, was I brave or was I reckless? What's the difference?' — leading into a discussion of when bold claims are warranted.

source.source_material: Dennett's Intuition Pumps Ch. 2 (Goulding) + PHIL 201 lecture notes

scenario.context: The player enters a heated village meeting in Thornfield. The council is debating whether to resettle three families from floodplain homes to higher ground. The move would save lives but requires demolishing an ancient burial grove sacred to the village's founders. Elder Sanna has just invoked the grove's sanctity. Councillor Breck wants to push forward with resettlement.
scenario.text: Breck lays out maps showing the flood risk. 'In the last five years, three floods. One child drowned. The floodplain homes will be underwater again — it's not a question of if but when. We have a clear plan to move these families to safe ground.' Elder Sanna rises. 'The grove is sacred. It has been sacred for four hundred years. Our ancestors are buried there. You do not dig up the dead for convenience. This conversation is over.' Breck throws up his hands. 'A child died, Sanna. Does the grove matter more than living children?' Sanna replies: 'Some things are not for calculation. That is what sacred means.' The room splits. No one knows how to continue.
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Sanna has deployed a conversation-stopper: an appeal to the sacred that forecloses further deliberation. Dennett and the W7 lecture notes on 'Thought Stoppers' identify these as moves that terminate reasoning by invoking a value held to be beyond discussion. Conversation-stoppers can be protective (preventing rash desecration) or destructive (preventing life-saving action). This scenario is genuinely dual — both sides have legitimate concerns.

structure.pattern_description: A conversation-stopper is any move that terminates deliberation by appeal to a value, right, rule, or taboo that is held to be non-negotiable. Dennett argues in 'Thought Stoppers' that these can be necessary (we do not deliberate about whether to torture innocents) but also dangerous (they can prevent needed moral progress). Sanna's appeal to sanctity shuts down cost-benefit reasoning entirely. This is dual-natured: the sanctity claim protects cultural heritage from thoughtless destruction, but it also blocks a life-saving measure from being discussed on its merits.
structure.formal_form: Agent A advances proposal P supported by reasons R. Agent B invokes value V, declared non-negotiable. B asserts: 'V overrides R; deliberation about P is inappropriate.' Deliberation halts. Whether this is good or bad depends on whether V truly should override R in this context — a question the stopper itself prevents from being asked.
structure.why_wrong: When a conversation-stopper blocks deliberation about life-and-death matters, it prevents the community from weighing all relevant values. Sanna's move makes it impossible to even discuss whether the families' safety and the grove's sanctity can both be honoured.
structure.why_right: Conversation-stoppers protect certain values from being eroded by incrementalist reasoning. Without them, every sacred site, every right, every moral boundary becomes negotiable, and the cumulative effect can be the loss of everything a community holds inviolable.
structure.counterpoint: The deepest challenge: how do you decide which conversation-stoppers to respect and which to override? That meta-question is itself a conversation that the stopper tries to prevent. Dennett suggests this is exactly where the Moral First Aid Manual is needed — a triage guide for when to honour the stopper and when to push past it.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sanna says 'This conversation is over.' Breck wants to keep talking. Who is right? Or is that the wrong question?

rubric.description: Player simply picks a side (grove or families) without recognizing the structural issue of the conversation-stopper.
Player senses a tension but frames it as a simple values conflict without seeing that Sanna's move is shutting down the deliberation itself.
Player recognizes that Sanna is ending the conversation and that this is a distinct move from arguing for the grove. But the player cannot articulate when such a move is appropriate.

Player identifies the conversation-stopper, explains its dual nature (protective and potentially harmful), and recognizes that the meta-question — when should deliberation be stopped? — is the real issue.

Player identifies the conversation-stopper, explains both its protective and obstructive functions, connects it to Dennett's thought-stoppers, and can propose a way to honour the grove's sanctity while still allowing deliberation about the families' safety — engaging with the meta-question of when stoppers should hold.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside for a moment who is right about the grove versus the families. Focus on Sanna's move: 'This conversation is over.' What kind of move is that? What does it do to the process of deliberation?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now the hardest version: can you think of a conversation-stopper that you believe should never be overridden? Something where ending the deliberation is genuinely the right thing to do? And then: how do you know the difference between that case and Sanna's?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elder Sanna is dignified, deeply principled, and speaks from genuine reverence — she is not being cynical. Councillor Breck is pragmatic, compassionate about the families, and frustrated by what he sees as dogma overriding safety. Both are good people in a genuine dilemma.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Sanna turns to you as you enter. 'Stranger, perhaps you can help settle this. They want to desecrate the founders' grove to build houses. I say some things are beyond discussion. Breck says everything is up for discussion. Which of us is right?' Breck adds quietly: 'A child drowned last spring.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: There is no clean win. If the player identifies the conversation-stopper and proposes a process — say, a staged deliberation that explicitly honours both values — the council agrees to continue talking. The player can suggest relocating the graves with ceremony, or building on adjacent land, or holding a community ritual to formally ask the ancestors' permission. The key insight is that the conversation-stopper was preventing the community from discovering creative solutions.

source.source_material: Dennett - Thought Stoppers + W7 lecture notes on moral heuristics and satisficing

scenario.context: The player encounters a retired general named Kael in a mountain monastery. Kael spent his career making quick battlefield decisions using rules of thumb — 'never split your force,' 'hold the high ground,' 'reinforce success.' These heuristics served him well. Now, in retirement, he has been reading philosophy and has realized that his heuristics were imperfect — they sometimes led to suboptimal outcomes. He is paralyzed by a new dilemma.
scenario.text: Kael stares at a chessboard he hasn't touched in days. 'Here is my problem, traveller. For thirty years I made fast decisions using simple rules. They were not perfect, but they were good enough. They saved lives more often than not. Now I understand they were heuristics — shortcuts that sometimes fail. I see the failures clearly now. The village I didn't reinforce because my rule said to reinforce success elsewhere. The flank I didn't protect because my rule said never to split the force.' He pauses. 'So now I know my rules are imperfect. Should I abandon them? If I try to reason through every decision from scratch, I will be too slow — people will die while I calculate. But if I follow rules I now know are flawed, am I not being irrational? I know too much to trust my own shortcuts, but not enough to do without them.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kael is experiencing what we can call Wolf's Dilemma — the predicament of the reflective satisficer. Herbert Simon argued that bounded rationality requires satisficing: using good-enough heuristics rather than optimizing. But once you become aware that your heuristics are imperfect, you face a dilemma: override them (and lose their speed and reliability) or follow them (knowing they are flawed). This connects to Susan Wolf's work on moral saints and the limits of reflective perfection, and to W7's discussion of when to trust your moral heuristics.

structure.pattern_description: This is the fundamental tension in bounded rationality: heuristics work because they are fast and frugal, but once you become reflectively aware of their limitations, you face a meta-decision. Do you (a) override the heuristic and reason from scratch (gaining accuracy but losing speed and sometimes doing worse due to overthinking), or (b) follow the heuristic knowing it is imperfect (preserving its advantages but violating your own rational standards)? There is no clean resolution. This is why Dennett's Moral First Aid Manual approach matters: it is a heuristic for managing heuristics — a second-order satisficing strategy.
structure.formal_form: Agent A uses heuristic H that produces outcome O in situation S. H is correct in situations S1...Sn but incorrect in Sn+1...Sm. A becomes aware that H is imperfect. A now faces meta-choice: follow H (fast, usually right, but known to be sometimes wrong) or abandon H and compute from scratch (slow, cognitively expensive, and not guaranteed to be better). Neither option is clearly rational.
structure.why_wrong: Blindly following heuristics you know to be flawed can be a form of intellectual cowardice — refusing to engage your critical faculties when it matters.
structure.why_right: Heuristics encode accumulated wisdom. Abandoning them in favour of slow deliberation often leads to worse outcomes, not better ones. The research on expert decision-making shows that experts who override their trained intuitions frequently perform worse than those who trust them.
structure.counterpoint: The resolution may lie in a third option: develop better meta-heuristics for knowing when to trust your heuristics and when to override them. This is essentially what Dennett's Moral First Aid Manual is — not a replacement for heuristics, but a guide for when to deploy reflection and when to trust the shortcut.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kael says he knows too much to trust his rules but not enough to abandon them. Is he right that this is a genuine dilemma? Is there a way out?

rubric.description: Player says Kael should either always follow his rules or always abandon them — sees no genuine tension.
Player recognizes the tension but frames it as simple indecision rather than a structural problem of bounded rationality.
Player sees the dilemma: heuristics are imperfect but necessary. Can articulate the problem but cannot propose any resolution.

Player identifies the core structure — reflective awareness of heuristic limitations creates a meta-dilemma — and proposes that the answer might be meta-heuristics: rules about when to follow your rules.

Player articulates the full dilemma, connects it to bounded rationality and satisficing, proposes the meta-heuristic solution, and recognizes that this creates an infinite regress (meta-meta-heuristics?) that must eventually be stopped — connecting to conversation-stoppers and the Moral First Aid Manual as a practical resolution to the regress.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: Kael used his rules for thirty years and they mostly worked. Now he knows they sometimes fail. Does knowing they sometimes fail mean he should stop using them? What would happen if he tried to reason through every decision from scratch?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You've identified the dilemma and a possible resolution. But notice: your meta-heuristic ('know when to trust your heuristics') is itself a heuristic. What happens when you become aware that it is imperfect? Is there an infinite regress here, and if so, how do you stop it?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Kael is thoughtful, haunted, and genuinely searching. He is not self-pitying — he is a rigorous thinker who has run into a wall. He speaks with military precision but has developed philosophical depth in retirement. He respects anyone who takes the dilemma seriously rather than dismissing it.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Kael does not look up from the chessboard. 'I used to move pieces without thinking. Now I think about every piece and cannot move at all. My soldiers would say I have gone soft. But I think I have gone honest. The question is whether honesty and effectiveness can coexist.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: There is no clean victory. The player can help Kael see that the answer is not 'abandon heuristics' or 'ignore your knowledge' but 'build a triage guide for when to trust your heuristics and when to override them.' This is the entry point to the Moral First Aid Manual. Kael's chess pieces begin moving again — not with the old unreflective speed, but with a new, deliberate rhythm.

source.source_material: W7 lecture notes (satisficing, moral heuristics) + Dennett Moral First Aid Manual + Simon on bounded rationality

scenario.context: The player visits an inventor named Sable who builds mechanical automata — clockwork servants that can follow instructions. Her latest creation, the Brass Porter, can carry objects between rooms. But it has developed a catastrophic flaw. Sable is trying to explain the problem to the player.
scenario.text: Sable gestures at the Brass Porter, which stands frozen in a doorway holding a tray of cups. 'I told it: carry the tray from the kitchen to the dining hall. Simple, yes? It picked up the tray. Then it stopped. It started checking things. Is the floor still there? Will the walls stay up? Does gravity still work? Has the air become poisonous? It has ten thousand rules about what might change when it acts, and it tries to verify all of them before each step.' She sighs. 'So I built a second version. This one only checks things that are relevant to the task. It picked up the tray and walked. Then it walked through a fire that had started in the hallway, because fire was not on its list of things relevant to carrying trays. Now it is a puddle of brass.' She looks at the player. 'How do you decide what to pay attention to?'
scenario.speaker_context: Sable has independently discovered the Frame Problem, one of the deepest challenges in AI and cognitive science. The problem: after any action, almost everything stays the same, but some things change. An intelligent agent must determine which things to check and which to take for granted. Checking everything leads to paralysis. Checking nothing leads to disaster. The problem is dual: no known algorithm solves it cleanly, yet humans handle it effortlessly (mostly).

structure.pattern_description: The Frame Problem asks: how does a rational agent determine what has and has not changed as a result of an action? Version 1 of the Porter checks everything (the Hamlet problem — paralyzed by the attempt to verify all possible changes). Version 2 checks only pre-specified relevant items (the tunnel-vision problem — walks into fires because fire is not on the relevance list). Humans solve this effortlessly through what Dennett calls a vast web of background assumptions that are updated contextually and associatively, not by exhaustive verification. But we cannot articulate how we do it, and no one has programmed a computer to do it.
structure.formal_form: Action A occurs in world state W1, producing W2. W1 has properties {P1...Pn}. Most properties are unchanged (frame axioms). Some properties change (effect axioms). The Frame Problem: how does the agent determine which properties to re-evaluate without (a) checking all of them (intractable) or (b) pre-specifying a fixed list (brittle)?
structure.why_wrong: A system that ignores the frame problem — either by checking everything or by pre-specifying a fixed relevance list — will fail catastrophically: either through paralysis or through missing critical changes.
structure.why_right: The frame problem, once recognized, helps you understand why common sense is so hard to replicate, why AI systems fail in unexpected ways, and why your own background reasoning is more impressive than you realize. Recognizing it is the first step toward designing better systems and better thinking.
structure.counterpoint: Some philosophers argue the frame problem is an artefact of the logical/computational framework and dissolves once you adopt embodied, situated cognition. Others argue it remains deep even for embodied agents. The debate is unresolved, which is part of what makes it a genuine puzzle.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sable's two Porters each failed in opposite ways. What is the underlying problem they share, and why is it so hard to solve?

rubric.description: Player sees the Porters as just having different bugs and proposes a simple fix (e.g., 'add fire to the list').
Player recognizes the trade-off between checking too much and checking too little but does not see it as a deep structural problem.
Player articulates the dilemma: you cannot check everything and you cannot pre-specify what to check. But does not connect this to the broader problem of common-sense reasoning.
Player identifies the Frame Problem: the challenge of determining what is relevant to re-evaluate after any action. Recognizes that both Porters fail because they lack a solution to this problem.

Player identifies the Frame Problem, explains both failure modes (paralysis and tunnel vision), notes that humans solve it through some unknown mechanism of background assumption management, and recognizes this as an open problem in AI and philosophy of mind with implications for how we think about intelligence itself.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose you add fire to the Porter's list. Problem solved? What about poison gas? Collapsing floors? Hostile animals? How long does the list get? And who decides what goes on it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You solved the puzzle — or rather, you identified why it is unsolved. Now turn it on yourself: you navigate the world effortlessly, somehow checking the right things and ignoring the irrelevant ones. How do you do it? Can you articulate your method? And if you cannot, what does that tell you about the nature of your own intelligence?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Sable is brilliant, frustrated, and slightly manic from sleepless nights wrestling with the problem. She speaks rapidly, illustrates points with mechanical diagrams, and gets genuinely excited when someone understands the depth of the problem rather than proposing surface fixes.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Sable is elbow-deep in clockwork when you enter. 'Don't tell me to add fire to the list. The last seven visitors said that. Here is the real question: how do you know what to add to the list? How do you know what you don't know? Answer that and you've solved the hardest problem in all of artifice.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: There is no full resolution — the Frame Problem is genuinely open. The player earns credit by recognizing its depth. Sable offers a partial workaround for the Porter: a set of general alarm conditions (heat, impact, novel obstacles) that function as crude meta-heuristics. She acknowledges it is a patch, not a solution. This connects to Wolf's Dilemma: the Porter now has heuristics it cannot fully justify, just like Kael.

source.source_material: Dennett's Intuition Pumps (Cognitive Wheels, the Frame Problem) + W7 lecture notes + PHIL 201 notes on AI and reasoning

scenario.context: The player has reached the Crossroads Monastery, the hub connecting all three learning tracks. Abbess Thera, the monastery's leader, is not a cleric but a retired judge who spent decades resolving impossible disputes. She has assembled a collection she calls the Practical Guide — a leather-bound book of decision procedures, ordered by urgency. A young monk named Dav has come to her in distress.
scenario.text: Dav is shaking. 'Abbess, I don't know what to do. My friend Luca stole medicine from the apothecary to save his dying mother. The apothecary is furious and wants Luca jailed. Luca's mother will die without the medicine. The town says stealing is wrong. My heart says Luca is right. But my teacher says you cannot build morality on feelings. Who is correct? Which moral theory do I follow — the one that says theft is always wrong, or the one that says save a life at any cost?' Abbess Thera opens her leather-bound Guide. 'You are asking the wrong question, Dav. You are asking which moral theory is the one true theory. There is no one true theory. Let me show you something more useful.'
scenario.speaker_context: Abbess Thera is about to introduce Dennett's Moral First Aid Manual — the idea that instead of searching for a single correct moral theory, we should build a practical triage guide that draws on multiple theories for different situations. Like a medical first aid manual, it does not resolve deep theoretical disputes (germ theory vs. miasma theory) — it tells you what to do right now, in order of urgency, while acknowledging uncertainty.

structure.pattern_description: Dennett proposes that instead of waiting to resolve the centuries-old debate between consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, and other moral theories, we should build a practical guide — a Moral First Aid Manual. Just as a medical first aid manual tells you to stop bleeding before diagnosing the underlying condition, a moral first aid manual provides triage procedures: (1) identify the most urgent moral consideration, (2) apply the most widely agreed-upon principle first, (3) escalate to more contested principles only when necessary, (4) acknowledge when you are in genuinely disputed territory and proceed with humility. This is satisficing applied to ethics — not the theoretically perfect answer, but a good-enough answer delivered in time to matter.
structure.formal_form: Situation S involves competing moral considerations {C1, C2, ...Cn} and competing moral theories {T1, T2, ...Tm} that rank C differently. Rather than resolving which T is correct, the Manual provides a triage procedure: (1) Identify the most urgent C. (2) Check for convergence: do multiple T agree on what to do? If yes, act. (3) If T disagree, identify the least controversial action that addresses the most urgent C. (4) Document the remaining disagreement for further reflection. (5) Revisit and refine the Manual based on outcomes.
structure.why_right: The Moral First Aid Manual is valuable because it is honest about theoretical disagreement while remaining practical. It does not pretend to solve metaethics — it acknowledges that smart, thoughtful people disagree about which moral theory is correct. But it insists that this disagreement should not paralyze us when people are suffering and decisions must be made. It is bounded rationality applied to ethics: satisfice now, optimize later.
structure.counterpoint: Critics might argue that a triage guide without a grounding theory is just unprincipled compromise. But Dennett's point is that the guide itself can be reflectively refined over time — it is a living document, not a fixed code. And the alternative (waiting for theoretical consensus before acting) has an unacceptable human cost.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dav wants to know which moral theory to follow. Abbess Thera says he is asking the wrong question. What does she mean, and what is the alternative she is proposing?

rubric.description: Player thinks Dav should just pick a moral theory and follow it, or that the Abbess is being evasive.
Player understands that the Abbess is saying multiple theories have value, but frames this as mere relativism — 'all theories are equal.'
Player grasps that the Abbess is proposing a practical approach rather than a theoretical one, but cannot articulate how the Manual works as a triage procedure.

Player understands the Moral First Aid Manual: instead of resolving which theory is correct, build a practical triage guide that checks for convergence across theories and prioritizes urgent considerations. Apply the most widely agreed-upon response first.

Player articulates the Manual's triage procedure, connects it to satisficing and bounded rationality, explains why it is not relativism (it has structure and can be refined), and can apply it to Dav's dilemma: most theories agree that saving a life is urgent; theft can be remediated; therefore treat the mother first and address the property violation through restitution after.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about a medical first aid manual. When someone is bleeding, the manual does not say 'first, resolve the debate between germ theory and humoral theory.' It says 'apply pressure to the wound.' Why? And can we do the same thing for moral emergencies?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You've grasped the Manual. Now stress-test it: what happens when the theories do not converge? When one theory says 'absolutely do X' and another says 'absolutely do not-X'? Does the Manual have a procedure for that, or does it break down? This is where the hard work begins.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Abbess Thera is calm, practical, and deeply experienced. She has no patience for abstract debate when someone is suffering, but she is also not anti-intellectual — she simply insists that theory must serve practice, not the other way around. She speaks in short, clear sentences and asks questions that cut to the core.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Thera looks up from her Guide as you enter. 'Another traveller with questions. Good. But I don't give answers — I give procedures. Tell me your situation, and I will tell you which question to ask first. Not the final question. The first one.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player helps Dav apply the Manual to his dilemma: (1) Most urgent consideration: Luca's mother is dying. (2) Convergence check: most moral frameworks agree that saving a life takes priority over property. (3) Action: return the medicine to Luca's mother, then negotiate restitution with the apothecary. (4) Remaining disagreement: was Luca justified in stealing? Document this for the Manual's ongoing refinement. Dav is relieved — not because the hard question is resolved, but because he has a procedure for acting while the hard question remains open. Thera adds a page to the Guide based on this case.

source.source_material: Dennett - The Moral First Aid Manual + W7 lecture notes + PHIL 201 lecture notes on moral reasoning

scenario.context: The player arrives at the gatehouse of Castle Thornwall seeking entry. A sign on the wall reads: 'If you carry a royal writ, you may pass.' The player does not have a royal writ.
scenario.text: Sergeant Dallow crosses his arms and nods at the sign. 'Rules are rules. The sign says if you carry a royal writ, you may pass. You don't have a royal writ. Therefore you may not pass. Turn around.'
scenario.speaker_context: Sergeant Dallow is a by-the-book guard who reads the gatehouse rule as though having a royal writ is the only way to gain entry. In fact, the castle also admits guild emissaries, healers during plague season, and anyone with a captain's token.

structure.pattern_description: Dallow reasons from 'If royal writ, then entry' and 'no royal writ' to 'no entry.' He treats the antecedent as necessary when the sign only establishes it as sufficient.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q.
structure.why_wrong: The conditional only tells us P is sufficient for Q, not necessary. Denying the antecedent does not validly yield the denial of the consequent. Other conditions may also lead to Q.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would be valid if the rule were biconditional: 'You may pass if and only if you carry a royal writ.' The fallacy lies in reading a one-way conditional as two-way.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sergeant Dallow seems confident in his logic. Look at the sign, then look at his reasoning. Does his conclusion actually follow?

rubric.description: Accepts Dallow's reasoning.
Feels something is wrong but cannot say what.
Notices that not having a writ might not mean you cannot enter, but cannot explain the logical error.
Identifies that Dallow treats a sufficient condition as necessary.
Names denying the antecedent, explains sufficient vs necessary conditions, and notes validity would require a biconditional.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The sign says having a writ is enough to get in. Does it say it is the only way? What is the difference?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now suppose the sign said: 'Only those carrying a royal writ may pass.' Would Dallow's reasoning be valid then? What changed?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Rigid, literal-minded, proud of his rule-following. Gets flustered when someone finds a loophole.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: No writ, no entry. That's what the sign says, and that's what I enforce.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the error and points out other valid credentials, Dallow grudgingly fetches the captain's handbook.

source.source_material: PHIL 201 lecture notes — sufficient vs necessary conditions

scenario.context: In Briarton, livestock have gone missing overnight. The village tracker, Wynn, examines paw prints near the sheep pen.
scenario.text: Wynn crouches beside the tracks. 'If a wolf attacked the sheep, we would find large paw prints near the pen. And look — large paw prints, right here. So it was a wolf. I will organize a hunting party at once.'
scenario.speaker_context: Wynn is a competent tracker but reasons too quickly. Large paw prints could come from a stray mastiff, a feral dog, or the lord's hound.

structure.pattern_description: Wynn reasons from 'If wolf then large paw prints' and 'large paw prints' to 'wolf.' She treats the consequent as proof of the antecedent.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Q. Therefore P.
structure.why_wrong: The conditional tells us a wolf attack would produce large paw prints, but many other causes could too. Observing Q does not allow us to conclude P.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would be valid if the conditional ran the other way: 'If large paw prints, then a wolf' — only if wolves were the sole possible source.

assessment.identification_prompt: Wynn seems sure it was a wolf. Does the conclusion follow from what she observed?

rubric.description: Agrees with Wynn.
Suspects she might be wrong but cannot explain why.
Notes tracks could belong to something else but does not identify the formal pattern.
Explains that Wynn reverses the conditional — paw prints are necessary if a wolf attacked, but not sufficient to prove it.
Names affirming the consequent, explains why direction of the conditional matters, and identifies what additional evidence is needed.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Is a wolf the only animal that leaves large prints? What else could have made those tracks?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Suppose Wynn said: 'Only wolves leave prints this large in Briarton.' Would her reasoning then be valid?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Sharp-eyed and action-oriented. Leaps to conclusions but respects players who slow her down with good reasoning.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Big prints, deep mud, torn fence. Wolf. Grab a spear — we leave within the hour.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out the gap, Wynn agrees to gather more evidence before raising the alarm.

source.source_material: PHIL 201 lecture notes — sufficient vs necessary conditions

scenario.context: At the Scholars' Hall, Researcher Tova has presented findings that a popular herbal supplement has no measurable effect on stamina. The merchant guild sends Guildmaster Holt to challenge her.
scenario.text: Guildmaster Holt stands: 'Consider what happens if people believe her. The redthorn harvesters lose their livelihoods. Three villages depend on the trade. Families will go hungry, children without schooling. Do we really want to accept a finding that would cause so much suffering?'
scenario.speaker_context: Holt does not address Tova's methods, data, or controls. He argues the conclusion should be rejected because accepting it would have undesirable economic consequences.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a factual claim should be rejected because accepting it would lead to undesirable outcomes, substituting the consequences for a critique of the evidence.
structure.formal_form: Claim P would have undesirable consequences C. Therefore P is false.
structure.why_wrong: The truth of a factual claim does not depend on whether its consequences are pleasant. Consequences are relevant to policy (what to do about a finding), not to whether the finding is true.
structure.counterpoint: Consequences can be legitimately relevant in policy decisions. Holt's concern for harvesters is valid as policy — but it has no bearing on whether the research is sound.

assessment.identification_prompt: Holt raises serious worries. But is he giving you any reason to doubt Tova's research itself?

rubric.description: Sides with Holt; bad consequences are reason enough to reject the finding.
Feels uneasy but cannot articulate why.
Notices Holt talks about economic effects rather than the study, but cannot separate the issues.
Identifies that Holt rejects the finding based on consequences rather than evidence.
Names the appeal to consequences, distinguishes evaluating evidence from making policy decisions.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose the redthorn trade employed nobody. Would Tova's study suddenly become more convincing?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Is there ever a legitimate reason to consider consequences when deciding what to do with a finding? How is that different from what Holt is doing?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Smooth-spoken, politically savvy, wraps self-interest in the language of compassion.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Before you side with the scholar, walk through the eastern hills. Look those harvesters in the eye and tell them their work means nothing.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy, the debate shifts from denying the research to planning around it, unlocking a quest to help the hill villages diversify.

source.source_material: PHIL 201 lecture notes — appeal to consequences

scenario.context: In Portmere, a dispute over whether a new dye works will poison the harbor fish. Fisherman Corvin cites expert testimony.
scenario.text: Corvin addresses the crowd: 'Master Eldric, the famous surgeon from the capital, examined the dye formulas and told me the chemicals will kill every fish in the harbor within a year. He is the most celebrated healer in three provinces. If a man of his stature says the dyes are toxic to fish, that settles it.'
scenario.speaker_context: Eldric is a renowned surgeon — an authority on human anatomy. Toxicology of industrial chemicals in marine environments is not his field.

structure.pattern_description: Corvin appeals to Eldric's authority as a surgeon to settle a question about marine toxicology — a field in which Eldric has no special expertise.
structure.formal_form: Authority A says P. A is expert in domain D. P is in domain D*. Therefore P is true. (But D ≠ D*.)
structure.why_wrong: An authority's expertise does not transfer automatically to unrelated domains. Eldric's prestige makes his opinion influential but not reliable on marine toxicology.
structure.counterpoint: Appealing to authority is not always fallacious. Citing a marine biologist on dye runoff would be reasonable. The fallacy lies in the mismatch between expertise and claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Corvin has a strong expert backing his claim. But what exactly is Eldric an expert in, and what is the question being debated?

rubric.description: Accepts Eldric's authority at face value.
Is unsure but cannot explain why Eldric's opinion might not be sufficient.
Notices Eldric is a surgeon, not a marine scientist, but does not articulate why that matters.
Identifies that Eldric's expertise is in surgery, not marine toxicology.
Names the appeal to irrelevant authority, explains the domain mismatch, and articulates when citing authority is legitimate.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose Eldric told you about performing surgery. Would you trust him? Now he's telling you about fish and industrial chemistry. Same kind of claim for him?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What if no marine toxicologist is available and Eldric is the most scientifically trained person in the region? Does that change how much weight we should give his opinion?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, weathered fisherman. Not trying to deceive — sought the most impressive expert he could find.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You would doubt Master Eldric? The man has saved more lives than you have drawn breaths.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Corvin admits he chose Eldric for fame rather than relevance. The council agrees to bring in a qualified assessor.

scenario.context: At the orphanage in Willowmere, the player has discovered the cook, Matron Geld, has been serving half-portions while selling surplus grain. Confronted with ledger evidence, Geld makes her case to the board.
scenario.text: Matron Geld clutches her apron: 'How dare you accuse me! Every winter I sit up through the night when they are sick. I held little Pip when his mother died. I braided Lila's hair for the harvest festival. And now you wave a ledger at me as if numbers matter more than love. Look at their faces — do these children look neglected? You should be ashamed.'
scenario.speaker_context: Geld deflects from concrete evidence by evoking pity for herself and guilt in her accusers. She does not contest the numbers.

structure.pattern_description: Substituting emotional response — pity, guilt, sentiment — in place of addressing the factual evidence. Geld does not contest the ledger; she tries to make accusers feel bad for asking.
structure.formal_form: Claim P is supported by evidence E. Agent evokes emotion F unrelated to E. Agent implies E should be disregarded because of F.
structure.why_wrong: Whether she sat up with sick children does not change what the grain ledger shows. The emotional response is designed to block the factual inquiry, not answer it.
structure.counterpoint: Emotions are not always irrelevant. Geld's service might bear on consequences (leniency), but that is about sentencing, not whether the skimming occurred.

assessment.identification_prompt: Matron Geld is clearly upset and has done real good. But does anything she says actually address the evidence in the ledger?

rubric.description: Is moved by Geld's speech and feels the accusation should be dropped.
Feels conflicted but cannot separate the emotional pull from the factual question.
Notices Geld did not address the ledger but struggles to explain why her emotional points are not valid defense.
Identifies Geld is using emotional appeals to deflect from factual evidence.
Names the appeal to emotion, distinguishes factual question from emotional one, explains when emotions would be legitimately relevant.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Set aside everything about the children. The ledger shows a gap between grain purchased and grain served. Has she explained that gap?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Suppose Geld had said 'I sold the surplus to buy medicine the board refused to fund.' That is also emotional but actually addresses the ledger. What makes one emotional appeal fallacious and another legitimate?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Warm, grandmotherly, genuinely devoted to the children — which makes her manipulation all the more effective.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You come into my kitchen with your columns of numbers and you think you know what happens here?
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the deflection and redirects to the ledger, the board agrees to audit the accounts.

scenario.context: A peddler named Saffron sells vials of plain spring water as a cure-all at the market in Dunmere. The local healer, Amara, has challenged him to explain what is in the vials.
scenario.text: Saffron holds up a vial: 'Nothing but pure mountain spring water — untouched by human hands, exactly as nature intended. That is why it works. Your body knows what is natural. These alchemical concoctions are brewed in workshops full of strange powders. My remedy comes straight from the earth. Natural means safe. Natural means it works with your body, not against it.'
scenario.speaker_context: Saffron offers no evidence of efficacy. The entire pitch rests on equating 'natural' with 'beneficial.'

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that a product works because it is natural, treating naturalness as sufficient evidence of safety and efficacy.
structure.formal_form: X is natural. What is natural is good/effective. Therefore X is good/effective.
structure.why_wrong: Naturalness is not a reliable indicator of safety or efficacy. Many natural substances are deadly (hemlock, arsenic). The appeal substitutes a feel-good category for actual evidence.
structure.counterpoint: There can be legitimate reasons to prefer less-processed substances, but that is a specific evidence-based argument, not a blanket claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Saffron's pitch sounds appealing. What evidence does he give that the spring water cures anything? Is 'it's natural' really a reason?

rubric.description: Finds the pitch convincing.
Is skeptical but cannot articulate why naturalness is insufficient.
Notes Saffron gives no real evidence but does not directly challenge the natural-equals-good assumption.
Identifies that Saffron equates naturalness with efficacy without evidence.
Names the appeal to nature, gives counterexamples of harmful natural substances, and distinguishes blanket claims from evidence-based preferences.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hemlock is natural. Nightshade is natural. Does 'natural' automatically mean safe?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Many people find this intuition appealing. Why? Is there a non-fallacious version of preferring natural products?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Charming, silver-tongued, genuinely believes in vaguely spiritual power of nature. Evasive when pressed for specifics.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Feel the weight of that vial. That is the weight of the mountain itself. No alchemist can brew what the earth gives freely.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy, Amara backs them up. Saffron agrees to submit his water for testing.

scenario.context: In Greenhollow during a festival, villagers line up to buy enchanted clover charms from vendor Paddy.
scenario.text: Paddy waves a charm: 'Look around you — half the village is wearing one already! Farmer Crewe bought three. The baker's whole family has them. Even old Magistrate Dunne picked one up. When this many people believe in something, there must be something to it. You don't want to be the only soul without one, do you?'
scenario.speaker_context: Paddy's entire pitch rests on the number of people who have already purchased. No evidence that charms bring fortune — just popularity.

structure.pattern_description: Arguing that something must be true or good because many people believe it or do it. Treating popularity as evidence.
structure.formal_form: Many people believe/do X. Therefore X is true/good.
structure.why_wrong: The number of people who believe something has no bearing on whether it is true. Popularity can be driven by social pressure, marketing, or tradition — none constitute evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Widespread adoption is not always irrelevant — independent expert convergence after separate investigation can be meaningful. But that is very different from festival-goers buying charms.

assessment.identification_prompt: What evidence does Paddy give that the charm works? Is 'everyone is buying one' a reason?

rubric.description: Finds the pitch convincing — if so many bought them, they must work.
Is hesitant but cannot explain why popularity is not good evidence.
Notes Paddy gives no real evidence but does not address the popularity-as-evidence move.
Identifies that Paddy uses number of buyers as sole evidence and explains popularity does not establish truth.
Names the bandwagon fallacy, explains why popularity is not evidence, identifies social pressure component, and distinguishes popularity from evidential convergence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose every person in the village believed the river flowed uphill. Would that make it true?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Is there any situation where the fact that many people believe something does give reason to take it seriously?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jovial, fast-talking festival vendor who thrives on crowd energy. Gets flustered when asked for actual evidence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Step right up! Everyone's got one — the farmer, the baker, the magistrate. You don't want to be the odd one out!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy, Bren the skeptical blacksmith offers the player a practical trade for helping settle another reasoning dispute.

scenario.context: A traveling merchant sells invisible amulets of protection, claiming they ward off curses.
scenario.text: You say my Amulet of Unseen Warding doesn't work? Well then, prove it! Go ahead — prove there ISN'T a magical barrier around you right now. You can't, can you? That's because it's working!
scenario.speaker_context: Merchant Orlo deflects every complaint by demanding the customer disprove his claims.

structure.pattern_description: Shifting the burden of proof from the person making the claim to the person questioning it.
structure.formal_form: P claims X. Q doubts X. P demands Q prove not-X, rather than P proving X.
structure.why_wrong: The person making a positive claim bears the responsibility of providing evidence. The inability to disprove something does not constitute evidence that it is true.
structure.counterpoint: What testable evidence can YOU provide that the amulet works? The claim is yours, so the proof must be yours.

assessment.identification_prompt: The merchant demands you prove his amulet doesn't work. What is wrong with this?

rubric.description: Tries to disprove the amulet.
Feels something is off but cannot articulate it.
Identifies that the merchant should provide proof, but cannot name the fallacy.
Identifies the burden of proof shift and explains the claimant must support their own claim.
Names the fallacy, explains why unfalsifiability is not evidence, connects to extraordinary claims requiring extraordinary evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If I told you there was a dragon in my cellar but you couldn't detect it — whose job is it to prove the dragon exists?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Are there situations where the burden of proof legitimately shifts? What about in a courtroom?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Theatrical, sweating slightly, always gesturing at empty air as though showing off invisible wares.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Finest protective charms in the realm — guaranteed or your... well, just guaranteed!
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player reports Orlo to the market magistrate, who requires a demonstration. Orlo packs up and leaves.

scenario.context: At the Naturalists' Guild, a senior ranger dismisses a young scholar's research on ancient fossils.
scenario.text: You're telling me those little fish-bones in the rock somehow turned into people? Walking, talking, thinking people came from FISH? I've been a ranger forty years and I've never seen a fish sprout legs. That's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard.
scenario.speaker_context: Ranger Harlen trusts his lived experience above all else and rejects any claim that defies his personal intuition.

structure.pattern_description: Dismissing a claim because one personally cannot understand or imagine how it could be true.
structure.formal_form: P cannot understand how X could be true. Therefore P concludes X is false.
structure.why_wrong: The complexity of a claim has no bearing on its truth. Many well-supported facts are deeply counterintuitive. Personal failure to comprehend is not a refutation.
structure.counterpoint: Does your difficulty imagining it mean it didn't happen, or that the process is more complex than everyday experience suggests?

assessment.identification_prompt: Ranger Harlen rejects the fossil evidence because he can't imagine fish becoming people. What error is he making?

rubric.description: Agrees with Harlen.
Recognizes he might be wrong but thinks experience counts as a valid counterargument.
Sees personal disbelief is not evidence but cannot name the pattern.
Identifies personal incredulity and explains that inability to understand does not refute evidence.
Names the fallacy, distinguishes emotional rejection from evidential refutation, notes that complex processes over vast timescales are inherently hard to intuit.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: There was a time when people couldn't believe the earth moved around the sun because they couldn't feel it. Was their experience a good reason to reject the evidence?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: When IS personal experience a legitimate reason to doubt a claim? What is the difference between incredulity and healthy skepticism?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff, weathered, deeply knowledgeable about wildlife but dismissive of book learning.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I know these woods better than any scholar knows their scrolls. You want to learn about nature? Walk with me.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player brings Harlen to coastal cliffs to examine a fossil sequence showing gradual skeletal changes. He grudgingly admits the pattern is hard to explain otherwise.

scenario.context: At the Diviner's Tower, a renowned psychic offers readings for gold. A skeptical mage proposes a controlled test.
scenario.text: My visions are real — I've helped hundreds! You want to test me? Fine. ...What, it didn't work? Well of course not, your skeptical energy was blocking my sight. True psychic ability doesn't function when hostile minds are present. That's not a failure; the conditions weren't right.
scenario.speaker_context: Seer Vashti has an explanation for every failed prediction and continually narrows the conditions under which her powers should work.

structure.pattern_description: When a claim is shown to be false, moving the goalposts by introducing ad hoc exceptions so the claim can never be falsified.
structure.formal_form: P claims X. Evidence against X is presented. P modifies X to X' by adding exception E so counter-evidence no longer applies.
structure.why_wrong: Each time counter-evidence appears, a new exception is added. This makes the claim unfalsifiable. A claim that cannot in principle be proven wrong is not meaningfully supported.
structure.counterpoint: Under what conditions WOULD you accept that your powers don't work? If no outcome counts as failure, claiming success is meaningless.

assessment.identification_prompt: Every time Seer Vashti's powers fail a test, she adds a new excuse. What reasoning error is this?

rubric.description: Accepts explanations — maybe skeptical energy really does interfere.
Suspects something is wrong but finds each individual excuse plausible.
Notices the pattern of retreating to new excuses but cannot name the fallacy.
Identifies special pleading and explains how moving goalposts makes the claim unfalsifiable.
Names the fallacy, articulates the unfalsifiability problem, explains why a legitimate claim must specify conditions under which it could be proven wrong.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Notice the pattern: first 'test me,' then 'not with skeptics,' then 'not under hostile conditions.' What would it take for Vashti to ever admit she was wrong?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Is there ever a legitimate reason to say conditions weren't right for an experiment? How do scientists distinguish genuine confounds from special pleading?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Serene, speaks in a soft melodic voice, becomes subtly defensive when challenged, always has one more excuse ready.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The spirits speak to me in whispers. Come, sit — let me show you what lies beyond the veil.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player proposes a double-blind test. When Vashti refuses or fails, the player confronts the pattern of excuses.

scenario.context: During a town council hearing, an ambitious alderman questions the local healer about a recent outbreak.
scenario.text: Tell me, Healer Maren — have you stopped using contaminated herbs in your remedies yet? The council deserves a straight answer: yes or no.
scenario.speaker_context: Alderman Greaves frames questions so that any direct answer implies guilt.

structure.pattern_description: A question containing a built-in assumption so that any direct answer appears to confirm it.
structure.formal_form: P asks 'Have you stopped doing X?' where X is unestablished. 'Yes' implies you were doing X. 'No' implies you still are.
structure.why_wrong: The question presupposes something not established — that Maren used contaminated herbs. Both yes and no accept the false premise.
structure.counterpoint: Maren should say: 'I reject the premise. You have not established that I ever used contaminated herbs. Present your evidence first.'

assessment.identification_prompt: Alderman Greaves demands a yes-or-no answer. What is the problem with this question?

rubric.description: Thinks Maren should just answer yes or no.
Feels the question is unfair but cannot explain why.
Notices the question assumes guilt but cannot name the technique.
Identifies it as a loaded question and explains the built-in assumption.
Names the loaded question, explains the embedded presupposition and false dilemma structure, suggests how to reject the premise.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Try answering both ways. If Maren says 'yes,' what does that imply? If 'no'?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: In everyday life, how do you recognize a loaded question? What are the telltale signs?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Smooth-voiced, politically savvy, uses formal address to disguise verbal traps.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I serve this council with nothing but the pursuit of truth. Now then, let us get to the heart of the matter...
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player objects to the question's framing. The council chair sustains the objection.

scenario.context: A traveling alchemist presents data to the village council claiming his tonic cures disease.
scenario.text: Behold my research! I surveyed thirty villages that drink my tonic. In five, the pox rate dropped dramatically last season. Five villages! I've circled those five on my map — the evidence speaks for itself.
scenario.speaker_context: Alchemist Rendell highlights only the data clusters supporting his claim, ignoring the twenty-five villages where nothing improved.

structure.pattern_description: Cherry-picking data clusters that suit a conclusion while ignoring data that does not. Like painting a target around bullet holes after shooting.
structure.formal_form: P observes a large dataset. P selects subset S supporting conclusion C while ignoring the rest.
structure.why_wrong: Finding a cluster in a large dataset is virtually guaranteed by chance. Selecting after the fact and presenting as evidence is statistically invalid. Honest analysis requires looking at ALL the data.
structure.counterpoint: What happened in the other twenty-five villages? Did you predict WHICH villages would improve before looking at the data?

assessment.identification_prompt: The alchemist tested in thirty villages but only shows five. What reasoning error is he committing?

rubric.description: Finds the five-village evidence convincing.
Thinks five seems small but cannot explain why the presentation is misleading.
Recognizes ignoring other villages is a problem but cannot name the fallacy.
Identifies cherry-picking / Texas sharpshooter and explains post-hoc selection.
Names the fallacy, explains prediction vs post-hoc pattern selection, discusses base rates, notes random variation would produce clusters by chance.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine throwing thirty darts randomly. Wouldn't some cluster together? Now draw a circle around the cluster and claim you were aiming there.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How would a proper test be designed? What would you need to demonstrate the tonic actually works?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Enthusiastic, uses colorful charts, speaks rapidly, glosses over inconvenient details.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Science, my friends! The numbers don't lie — well, the numbers I'm showing you don't lie!
