Player does all the above and notes the tradeoff: replacing 'most' with 'all' makes the argument deductively valid but gives it a false premise, while 'most' makes the premise defensible but the conclusion defeasible.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Focus on the word 'most' versus 'all.' The mathematician says ALL birds fly — so the conclusion follows with certainty. The naturalist says MOST birds fly — so the conclusion follows with probability. Now add a new fact. Which type of argument can be weakened by new information?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider: in everyday reasoning, which type of argument do we use more often? If most of our reasoning is inductive and defeasible, what does that mean for how confident we should be in our conclusions?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The mathematician is precise and absolute; she deals in certainties. The naturalist is empirical and cautious; he updates his beliefs when new evidence arrives. Their contrasting styles embody the deductive-inductive distinction.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The mathematician says: 'My argument is airtight — IF the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.' The naturalist says: 'My argument was good until we learned more. That is not a flaw — that is how evidence-based reasoning works.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correctly explaining defeasibility earns the player a 'Defeasibility Lens' — an in-game tool that highlights when an NPC's argument is deductive vs inductive and flags when new evidence might weaken an inductive argument.

scenario.context: It is election season in Millhaven. Two rival pollsters have each surveyed voters about the upcoming mayoral race. The player, serving as the town's logic clerk, must evaluate the quality of each poll.
scenario.text: Pollster A says: 'I asked 20 people at the Miners' Guild hall and 15 said they will vote for Candidate X. That is 75% support — X will win in a landslide!' Pollster B says: 'I randomly selected 500 residents from the full census roll — merchants, miners, farmers, anglers — and 52% said they will vote for Candidate X. It looks like a close race.' The scribe asks: 'Which poll should the council trust, and why?'
scenario.speaker_context: This is directly from Bert's lecture notes on statistical generalizations, sample size, and sampling bias. Pollster A commits the fallacy of hasty generalization (too-small sample from a biased location), while Pollster B uses random sampling from a larger, more representative pool.

structure.pattern_name: Statistical generalizations: sample size and representativeness
structure.pattern_description: A good statistical generalization requires two conditions: adequate sample size and a representative sample. Pollster A fails both: 20 people is too few (hasty generalization), and surveying only at the Miners' Guild creates a biased sample that likely overrepresents mining interests. Pollster B uses random selection from the full census (avoiding selection bias) and surveys 500 people (much more adequate sample size). The two conditions work together: even a large sample is useless if biased, and even a representative method is unreliable with too few participants.
structure.formal_form: Statistical generalization: X% of sample S has property P. Therefore, approximately X% of population has property P. Conditions: (1) S is large enough (adequate sample size). (2) S is representative of the population (random sampling, no selection bias). Pollster A: fails both. Pollster B: satisfies both.
structure.why_right: Evaluating statistical generalizations requires checking sample size and representativeness. Pollster A's survey is doubly flawed: 20 people is too small to generalize from (the result could easily be due to chance), and surveying at the Miners' Guild selects for a specific demographic that may not reflect the town as a whole. Pollster B's random sampling from the census roll ensures that every type of resident has an equal chance of being surveyed, and 500 is a much more adequate sample size.
structure.counterpoint: Even random sampling can go wrong if the response rate is low (non-response bias) or if the questions are loaded. And sample size adequacy depends on the population size and the margin of error you need — 500 might not be enough for a very large city.

assessment.identification_prompt: The scribe asks you to evaluate both polls. Which one should the council trust, and what are the problems with the other one?

rubric.description: Player accepts Pollster A's result because the percentage is higher, or cannot identify any methodological issues.
Player senses that Pollster A's result is less reliable but can only name one issue (sample size or bias, not both).
Player identifies both the sample size problem and the sampling bias in Pollster A's survey, but does not articulate the general conditions for a good statistical generalization.
Player identifies both problems, explains the two conditions (adequate sample size and representativeness), and explains why Pollster B's method is superior.
Player does all the above and notes potential weaknesses even in Pollster B's approach (response rate, question wording) and explains the concept of hasty generalization.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine you want to know what all of Millhaven thinks. Would you only ask people in one guild hall? How many people would you need to ask to feel confident? Those two questions point to the two conditions.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider: Pollster B's survey also found that 90% of respondents think the town needs a new bridge. But the survey was conducted at the market, where people have to cross the old bridge. Is there a problem?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The town scribe is skeptical and data-literate. She has seen too many council decisions driven by bad polls and wants the player to develop the same skepticism. She speaks with dry precision.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Every election season, someone surveys their friends and calls it a poll. Twenty people at a guild hall is not a poll — it is a conversation with selection bias. Tell me which of these two surveyors actually did the work.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correctly evaluating the polls earns the player access to the Census Archives, where they can examine real demographic data for Millhaven and design their own unbiased surveys for future quests.

scenario.context: A merchant's warehouse in Salthaven has been found empty — the goods vanished overnight with no sign of forced entry. Three investigators each propose a different explanation. The player, acting as magistrate, must evaluate which explanation is best using the explanatory virtues.
scenario.text: Inspector Lira says: 'The goods were teleported away by a rogue mage. That would explain the lack of forced entry.' Inspector Gareth says: 'The night watchman sold the goods out the back door and is lying about the theft. He has the only key, he has gambling debts, and the wagon tracks behind the warehouse match the route to the black market district.' Inspector Nessa says: 'The goods were taken by the same gang that hit the Harbor District last month. They have been known to bribe watchmen, and the pattern matches — high-value goods, no entry signs, inside knowledge of guard schedules.'
scenario.speaker_context: The player must compare three competing explanations using IBE (inference to the best explanation) and the seven explanatory virtues: testability, scope, simplicity, mechanism, fruitfulness, consistency with background knowledge, and explanatory power.

structure.pattern_name: Inference to the best explanation and explanatory virtues
structure.pattern_description: IBE selects the hypothesis that best explains the observed evidence according to the explanatory virtues. Lira's explanation (teleportation by rogue mage) is unfalsifiable, inconsistent with background knowledge, and introduces unnecessary entities — it fails on simplicity, testability, and consistency. Gareth's explanation (watchman as inside thief) is simple, testable (check his finances, interview wagon drivers), and has strong explanatory power (explains lack of forced entry, opportunity, motive). Nessa's explanation (organized gang) has broader scope (explains multiple thefts) and is fruitful (predicts future targets), but introduces more actors and is slightly less parsimonious for this single case. Both Gareth and Nessa offer good IBEs; Lira's fails on multiple virtues.
structure.formal_form: Evidence E: goods vanished, no forced entry, watchman reports theft. H1 (Lira): teleportation by mage. H2 (Gareth): watchman is the thief. H3 (Nessa): organized gang bribed watchman. IBE selects H that best satisfies: testability, scope, simplicity, mechanism, fruitfulness, consistency, explanatory power. H1 fails testability, simplicity, consistency. H2 scores high on simplicity, testability, mechanism. H3 scores high on scope and fruitfulness.
structure.why_right: IBE is not about which explanation is merely possible — all three are possible. It is about which explanation does the best job of accounting for the evidence according to the explanatory virtues. Lira's hypothesis explains the evidence but at the cost of invoking an extraordinary mechanism with no independent support. Gareth's and Nessa's both provide natural mechanisms and testable predictions. The choice between them depends on whether we weight simplicity (Gareth) or scope and fruitfulness (Nessa).
structure.counterpoint: IBE is not deductively valid — the best explanation might still be wrong. New evidence could favor a different hypothesis. And the virtues can conflict: the simplest explanation is not always the one with the broadest scope. Judgment is required.

assessment.identification_prompt: Three investigators each offer an explanation. Evaluate each one using the explanatory virtues. Which is the best explanation, and why?

rubric.description: Player accepts one explanation without comparing it to the others or considering the explanatory virtues.
Player rejects Lira's explanation as implausible but cannot articulate why using the virtues framework.
Player correctly identifies Lira's explanation as worst and picks either Gareth or Nessa, but uses only one or two virtues in the evaluation.
Player evaluates all three explanations against multiple explanatory virtues and provides a well-reasoned ranking.
Player does all the above, notes the tradeoff between simplicity and scope in comparing Gareth and Nessa, and acknowledges that IBE is defeasible — new evidence could shift the ranking.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Start with Lira's explanation. Could you test it? Does it fit with what you already know about the world? Now compare: Gareth's explanation gives you specific things to check — the watchman's finances, the wagon tracks. Which explanation gives you more to work with?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good analysis. Now suppose new evidence arrives: three more warehouses in other towns were hit the same way. Does that change your ranking of Gareth vs Nessa? Why? This is what defeasibility looks like in explanatory reasoning.

game_hooks.npc_personality: The magistrate (player's role) is expected to be judicious and methodical. Lira is credulous and dramatic. Gareth is blunt and evidence-focused. Nessa is strategic and pattern-oriented.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Gareth drops a ledger on the table. 'Check his debts. Check the wagon tracks. I can show you the evidence.' Nessa unfolds a map with three other warehouse locations circled. 'This is bigger than one watchman.' Lira waves dismissively. 'You are both thinking too small. No mundane explanation accounts for zero evidence of entry.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player ranks the explanations and justifies their choice. If they rank well, they are assigned to investigate further — Gareth's lead opens a detective quest, Nessa's opens a conspiracy quest. Both teach further reasoning skills.

scenario.context: The player encounters a philosopher in the town square who is making a provocative moral argument. A merchant named Aldric has just refused to donate to a famine relief fund, saying it is not his responsibility. The philosopher challenges Aldric using an analogy.
scenario.text: The philosopher says: 'Consider this, Aldric. A child is drowning in a shallow pond. You could easily wade in and save her, but you would ruin your expensive boots. Would you let the child drown to save your boots? No? Then why do you spend five gold every day on coffee and pastries when that same money could save a child's life through the famine relief fund? The situations are analogous — in both cases, you are choosing a luxury over a child's survival.' Aldric replies: 'Those situations are nothing alike! The child in the pond is right in front of me. The famine is on another continent. And my coffee money alone will not solve a systemic famine.'
scenario.speaker_context: This is adapted from Bert's lecture notes on argument by analogy, using the classic Peter Singer / Bob's expensive car scenario. The key question is whether the similarities between the two cases are relevant to the conclusion, and whether the disanalogies Aldric raises are legitimate or evasive.

structure.pattern_name: Argument by analogy: relevant similarities and disanalogies
structure.pattern_description: An argument by analogy infers that because two things share relevant similarities, what is true of one is probably true of the other. The philosopher argues: (1) The pond case and the coffee case share a relevant similarity — choosing a luxury over a child's survival. (2) In the pond case, saving the child is clearly obligatory. (3) Therefore, donating the coffee money is obligatory. Aldric raises two disanalogies: physical proximity (the pond child is right there) and efficacy (one person's donation cannot solve a systemic problem). The quality of the analogy depends on whether these disanalogies are relevant to the moral conclusion.
structure.formal_form: Analogy: Case A (pond) and Case B (coffee) share property S (choosing luxury over child's survival). In Case A, moral verdict V holds (you should save the child). Therefore, in Case B, V probably holds (you should donate). Counterargument: Cases A and B differ in properties D1 (proximity) and D2 (efficacy). If D1 or D2 is relevant to V, the analogy weakens.
structure.why_right: Evaluating analogies requires identifying the relevant similarities and assessing whether the disanalogies matter. The philosopher's analogy is strong because the core moral feature — valuing a luxury over a child's life — is the same in both cases. Proximity may be psychologically compelling but is morally questionable as a distinguishing factor: does a child's life matter less because they are far away? The efficacy objection is stronger: in the pond case, your action directly saves the child, while in the famine case, your donation is a drop in a systemic bucket. The best analogical arguments invoke similarities that are directly relevant to the conclusion.
structure.counterpoint: Aldric's disanalogies are worth taking seriously, especially the systemic one. The pond analogy may succeed in showing that proximity is not morally relevant, but it does not address the question of whether individual action is effective against structural problems. A stronger version of Aldric's objection would argue for institutional rather than individual solutions.

assessment.identification_prompt: The philosopher draws an analogy between the drowning child and the daily coffee purchase. Is it a good analogy? Evaluate the relevant similarities and the disanalogies Aldric raises. Which disanalogies, if any, are relevant to the moral conclusion?

rubric.description: Player accepts or rejects the analogy without examining the similarities and differences.
Player identifies one similarity or one disanalogy but does not systematically evaluate the analogy.
Player identifies the core similarity and at least one disanalogy but does not assess whether the disanalogy is relevant to the moral conclusion.
Player identifies the relevant similarity (luxury vs child's life), evaluates both disanalogies, and argues that proximity is less relevant than efficacy.

Player does all the above, explains the general conditions for a strong argument by analogy (relevant similarities must bear on the conclusion), and distinguishes weak disanalogies (proximity) from strong ones (systemic efficacy).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Start with the similarity: in both cases, someone is choosing a luxury item over a child's survival. Now look at the differences Aldric raises. For each one, ask: does this difference actually change whether you have a moral obligation? Or is it just an excuse?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good analysis. The philosopher used a deliberately extreme case (drowning child) to pump the intuition, then transferred it to the everyday case. This is what Dennett calls an 'intuition pump.' Can you think of a case where this technique goes wrong — where the pump generates a misleading intuition?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The philosopher is provocative and Socratic — she does not tell you the answer but forces you to find it by examining the analogy. Aldric is defensive but not unreasonable; his objections have some merit. The tension is genuine.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The philosopher turns to you. 'Aldric thinks the pond and the coffee shop are nothing alike. I think the only difference is that the pond makes you uncomfortable and the coffee shop does not. Which of us is right?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player produces a strong analysis, the philosopher offers to teach them the 'Analogy Lens' — an in-game tool for evaluating analogies by mapping relevant similarities. Aldric, if his systemic objection is validated, proposes a town-wide tax for famine relief instead.

scenario.context: A veterinarian in the village of Fenhollow has been tracking seizures in a cat named Whiskers. She has recorded which conditions were present on days when Whiskers had seizures versus days when Whiskers did not. The player helps her apply Mill's methods to identify the cause.
scenario.text: The vet presents her log: 'Seizure Day 1: new food (F), thunderstorm (T), visitor present (V). Seizure Day 2: new food (F), no thunderstorm, visitor present (V). Seizure Day 3: new food (F), thunderstorm (T), no visitor. No-seizure Day 1: old food, thunderstorm (T), visitor present (V). No-seizure Day 2: old food, no thunderstorm, no visitor.' She asks: 'Which factor is the cause of the seizures? Use the necessary condition test and the sufficient condition test.'
scenario.speaker_context: This is directly adapted from Bert's lecture notes on causal reasoning and Mill's methods, using his cat seizure example. The necessary condition test asks: which factor is present every time the effect occurs? The sufficient condition test asks: which factor is never present when the effect is absent?

structure.pattern_name: Mill's methods: necessary and sufficient condition tests
structure.pattern_description: The necessary condition test: which factor is present in every seizure case? F is present in all three seizure days. T is present in days 1 and 3 but not day 2. V is present in days 1 and 2 but not day 3. Only F passes the necessary condition test. The sufficient condition test: which factor is absent in every non-seizure case? F is absent in both non-seizure days. T is present in no-seizure day 1, so T alone is not sufficient. V is present in no-seizure day 1, so V alone is not sufficient. F passes both tests: it is present in every seizure case and absent in every non-seizure case.
structure.formal_form: Necessary condition test: factor X is a necessary condition for effect E if X is present whenever E is present. Sufficient condition test: factor X is a sufficient condition for E if E is absent whenever X is absent (equivalently, E is present whenever X is present). Data: F passes both. T fails necessary (absent in seizure day 2). V fails necessary (absent in seizure day 3). T fails sufficient (present in no-seizure day 1). V fails sufficient (present in no-seizure day 1).
structure.why_right: Mill's methods provide systematic tools for causal investigation. The necessary condition test eliminates factors that are absent when the effect occurs. The sufficient condition test eliminates factors that are present when the effect does not occur. Only the new food (F) survives both tests, making it the strongest candidate cause. However, these tests require factors to be wholly present or absent — they cannot handle dose-dependent effects or concomitant variation.
structure.counterpoint: Rigorous testing means actively looking for situations where a candidate fails one of the tests. It is also possible that factors are jointly sufficient but not individually sufficient — F might only cause seizures in combination with another factor, though the data here does not support that.

assessment.identification_prompt: Using the vet's log, apply the necessary condition test and the sufficient condition test to each factor. Which factor is the likely cause of Whiskers' seizures?

rubric.description: Player guesses a factor without applying any systematic test.
Player applies one test (necessary or sufficient) but not both, or applies a test incorrectly.
Player correctly applies both tests but makes an error in one case (e.g., does not notice that T fails the necessary test because it is absent in seizure day 2).
Player correctly applies both tests to all three factors and identifies F as the cause.

Player does all the above and discusses limitations: the need for rigorous testing, the possibility of jointly sufficient causes, and the fact that these tests require binary present/absent conditions.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Start with the necessary condition test. Look at seizure day 2: there was no thunderstorm. So can the thunderstorm be a necessary condition for seizures? What factor was present in ALL three seizure days?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now the vet adds a new observation: on a day when Whiskers ate the new food but was also given a calming supplement, no seizure occurred. What does that tell you? Is the new food really sufficient by itself, or might there be a more complex causal picture?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The vet is methodical, caring, and scientifically minded. She treats her cat's health like a research problem and welcomes the player's help in applying systematic methods.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I have been keeping this log for weeks and I can see a pattern, but I want to make sure I am not jumping to conclusions. Help me test each factor properly — necessary condition test first, then sufficient condition test.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correct analysis earns the player a 'Causal Investigator' badge and unlocks a more complex causal reasoning quest involving concomitant variation and correlation vs causation.

scenario.context: The town council of Millhaven is reviewing a report claiming that a new health tonic causes improved crop yields. The evidence: farms whose workers drink the tonic have 20% higher yields than farms whose workers do not. The player, serving as logic clerk, must evaluate the causal claim.
scenario.text: Councillor Drava presents the report: 'The data are clear. Farms where workers drink Vigor Tonic produce 20% more grain. The tonic must be making the workers more productive. I move that the council subsidize Vigor Tonic for all farm workers.' The town physician objects: 'Wait. Has anyone considered that the farms with higher yields are the wealthier farms? Wealthier farmers can afford both better equipment and the tonic. The tonic might have nothing to do with the yields.' A third voice adds: 'Or maybe the causation runs the other way — workers on high-yield farms earn more and spend it on the tonic.'
scenario.speaker_context: This illustrates the three alternatives to a direct causal explanation when A and B are positively correlated: (1) A causes B, (2) B causes A (reverse causation), (3) a third variable C causes both A and B (confounding). This is directly from Bert's lecture notes on correlation vs causation.

structure.pattern_name: Correlation vs causation: third variable and reverse causation
structure.pattern_description: When two things are positively correlated, there are four logical possibilities: (1) A causes B, (2) B causes A, (3) a third variable C causes both, (4) the correlation is coincidental. Drava assumes possibility 1 (tonic causes higher yields). The physician raises possibility 3 (wealth is the confounding variable — it causes both tonic purchase and better yields through equipment). The third voice raises possibility 2 (higher yields cause higher income, which causes tonic purchase). Inferring causation from mere correlation commits the false cause fallacy (post hoc fallacy).
structure.formal_form: Correlation: farms with tonic (A) correlate with higher yields (B). Possibilities: (1) A -> B (tonic causes yields). (2) B -> A (yields cause tonic purchase). (3) C -> A and C -> B (wealth causes both). (4) Coincidence. Drava commits the false cause fallacy by assuming (1) without eliminating (2), (3), and (4).
structure.why_right: Recognizing that correlation does not establish causation is essential for evaluating empirical arguments. To establish causation, you need to rule out confounding variables and reverse causation — typically through controlled experiments or careful statistical analysis. Background knowledge (IBE) can help determine which causal direction is most plausible, but mere positive correlation is never sufficient by itself.
structure.counterpoint: Correlation is not worthless — it is often the starting point for causal investigation. And sometimes background knowledge makes one causal direction far more plausible than others. The error is not in noticing correlations but in leaping from correlation to causation without further investigation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councillor Drava claims the tonic causes higher yields based on the correlation data. What is wrong with this inference? Identify the alternative explanations.

rubric.description: Player accepts Drava's causal claim without question.
Player senses something is wrong but can only vaguely articulate the problem.
Player identifies one alternative explanation (either reverse causation or confounding) but not both.
Player identifies both reverse causation and the confounding variable explanation, and names the false cause fallacy.

Player does all the above, explains that correlation is necessary but not sufficient for causation, and suggests how you would test the causal claim (e.g., a controlled experiment providing tonic to randomly selected farms).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Here is a hint: wealthy farms can afford better equipment. Wealthy farms can also afford the tonic. Could wealth explain both the tonic use and the higher yields, without the tonic doing anything at all?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now visit tylervigen.com in the Guild archives — you will find that the number of films Nicolas Cage appeared in correlates with the number of people who drowned in swimming pools. Should we conclude that Nicolas Cage movies cause drownings? Why is this correlation obviously spurious, while the tonic correlation is not so obviously spurious?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Councillor Drava is well-meaning but data-naive. The physician is sharp and skeptical. Together they model the tension between acting on imperfect evidence and demanding better evidence before acting.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Drava waves the report. 'Twenty percent! You cannot argue with numbers!' The physician sighs. 'I am not arguing with the numbers. I am arguing with what you think the numbers mean.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the alternative explanations, the council votes to fund a controlled trial instead of a subsidy. This unlocks a quest to design the experiment, teaching experimental methodology.

scenario.context: The player visits a gambling house in Salthaven where a dice master is teaching probability to new dealers. The dice master presents a series of probability problems using six-sided dice and coins.
scenario.text: The dice master says: 'Three problems for you, dealer-in-training. First: what is the probability of NOT rolling a 4 on a fair six-sided die? Second: I flip two fair coins. What is the probability that at least one lands heads? Be careful — most people get this one wrong. Third: I roll a fair six-sided die six times. What is the probability of getting at least one 4? Do NOT just add up the individual probabilities — I have seen that mistake end careers.'
scenario.speaker_context: The dice master is teaching the complement rule, the addition rule (with correction for double-counting), and the proper way to compute 'at least one' probabilities using negation. These are directly from Bert's lecture notes, including his warning about the common error of adding probabilities.

structure.pattern_name: Basic probability laws: complement, addition, conjunction
structure.pattern_description: Problem 1 (complement): P(not-4) = 1 - P(4) = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6. Problem 2 (addition with correction): P(at least one H) = P(H on coin 1) + P(H on coin 2) - P(H on both) = 1/2 + 1/2 - 1/4 = 3/4. Alternatively, use complement: 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4. Problem 3 (at least one via complement): P(at least one 4 in 6 rolls) = 1 - P(no 4 in 6 rolls) = 1 - (5/6)^6 = approximately 0.665, NOT 6/6 = 1. The naive addition of 1/6 six times gives 100%, which is obviously wrong.
structure.formal_form: P(not-A) = 1 - P(A). P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). P(at least one A in n trials) = 1 - P(not-A)^n. Problem 1: 1 - 1/6 = 5/6. Problem 2: 1/2 + 1/2 - 1/4 = 3/4, or 1 - (1/2)^2 = 3/4. Problem 3: 1 - (5/6)^6 ≈ 0.665.
structure.why_right: The complement rule is the most useful tool in basic probability: often it is easier to calculate the probability of something NOT happening and subtract from 1. The addition rule must correct for double-counting when events can co-occur (the simple formula P(A) + P(B) counts the overlap twice). The 'at least one' calculation via complement is essential — the naive addition error (adding 1/6 six times to get 100%) violates the axiom that probabilities cannot exceed 1.
structure.counterpoint: These rules assume independent events. If events are dependent (e.g., drawing cards without replacement), the conjunction formula changes to P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B|A). The problems above use independent events for simplicity.

assessment.identification_prompt: Solve the three probability problems. Show your work and explain which probability law you use for each one.

rubric.description: Player cannot apply any probability laws or makes fundamental errors (e.g., claiming 6 rolls guarantees a 4).
Player correctly solves problem 1 but makes errors on problems 2 or 3, likely by failing to correct for double-counting or by naively adding probabilities.
Player solves problems 1 and 2 correctly but uses the naive addition method for problem 3, getting an answer greater than 1.
Player solves all three correctly using the appropriate laws and shows their work.
Player solves all three, explains why the naive addition fails (double-counting), demonstrates the complement method, and notes the independence assumption.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: For problem 3: if you add 1/6 six times, you get 1 — but that would mean you are guaranteed to roll a 4, which is clearly wrong. The error is double-counting. Instead, ask: what is the probability of NOT rolling a 4 in any of the six rolls? Then subtract that from 1.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now the dice master asks: 'What about rolling at least one 4 in 12 rolls?' Use the same method. And notice: no matter how many times you roll, can the probability ever actually reach 1?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The dice master is a grizzled veteran of the gambling trade who has seen every probability mistake in the book. He teaches with the urgency of someone who has watched fortunes lost to bad math.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I had a dealer once who told a customer the chance of rolling a 4 in six tries was 100%. The customer took that bet, lost, and came back with a very large friend. Learn the complement rule or learn to run fast.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correct answers earn the player a 'Probability Basics' certification and unlock the Bayes' Theorem challenge at the next table in the gambling house.

scenario.context: The player is in the Salthaven courthouse, where a witness identification case has come before the magistrate. An eyewitness has identified a suspect, and the player must evaluate how much this identification should update the probability of guilt.
scenario.text: The magistrate presents the case: 'Eyewitness Bob claims he saw Nancy commit the robbery. Bob's identification accuracy is 99% — he correctly identifies the perpetrator 99% of the time, and correctly clears innocent people 99% of the time. Sounds convincing, right?' She pauses. 'But consider: suppose 1000 people could have been in the area. Of those, about 5 are actual robbers and 995 are not. Now: given Bob's positive identification, what is the actual probability that Nancy is the robber?'
scenario.speaker_context: This is directly from Bert's lecture notes on the base rate fallacy, using his eyewitness testimony example. Despite Bob's 99% accuracy, the low base rate of actual robbers in the population means the probability is much lower than people intuitively expect.

structure.pattern_name: Conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, and base rate reasoning
structure.pattern_description: The naive answer is 99%, but this ignores the base rate. Using Bayes' theorem: Of 1000 people, 5 are robbers. Bob correctly identifies 99% of 5 robbers = 4.95 true positives. Bob incorrectly identifies 1% of 995 innocent people = 9.95 false positives. Total positive identifications = 4.95 + 9.95 = 14.9. P(Nancy is robber | Bob says yes) = 4.95 / 14.9 = approximately 33%. Despite Bob's 99% accuracy, it is more likely than not that Nancy is innocent.
structure.formal_form: P(Robber) = 5/1000 = 0.005. P(ID+ | Robber) = 0.99. P(ID+ | Not Robber) = 0.01. P(Robber | ID+) = P(ID+ | Robber) * P(Robber) / [P(ID+ | Robber) * P(Robber) + P(ID+ | Not Robber) * P(Not Robber)] = (0.99 * 0.005) / (0.99 * 0.005 + 0.01 * 0.995) = 0.00495 / 0.01490 ≈ 0.332 = 33.2%.
structure.why_right: Conditional probability requires updating prior probabilities with new evidence. The key insight is that when the base rate is low (few robbers in the population), even a highly accurate test produces many false positives relative to true positives. P(Robber | ID+) is NOT the same as P(ID+ | Robber). Confusing these two is called the prosecutor's fallacy. Bayes' theorem provides the correct way to update: multiply the base rate by the likelihood ratio.
structure.counterpoint: This does not mean eyewitness testimony is worthless — it raised the probability from 0.5% to 33%, a significant update. Additional independent evidence (a second witness, physical evidence) would further increase the probability. The lesson is not to dismiss evidence but to combine it properly with base rates.

assessment.identification_prompt: The magistrate asks: given Bob's 99% accuracy and 1000 people in the area with 5 actual robbers, what is the probability that Nancy is truly the robber? Show your reasoning.

rubric.description: Player answers 99% or close to it, falling for the base rate fallacy.
Player recognizes that the answer is lower than 99% but cannot compute the correct value.
Player sets up the problem correctly (identifying true positives and false positives) but makes arithmetic errors.
Player correctly computes approximately 33% and explains why the base rate matters.

Player does all the above, distinguishes P(ID+|Robber) from P(Robber|ID+), names the prosecutor's fallacy, and notes that the identification still significantly updated the probability from the base rate.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Let us count. Of the 5 actual robbers, Bob correctly identifies 99%, so about 4.95 true positives. Of the 995 innocent people, he incorrectly fingers 1%, so about 9.95 false positives. Total people Bob says are robbers: about 14.9. What fraction of those are actual robbers?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good Bayesian reasoning. Now the magistrate asks: suppose a second independent witness, also 99% accurate, also identifies Nancy. How does that change the calculation? Hint: Nancy's new base rate is now 33%, not 0.5%.

game_hooks.npc_personality: The magistrate is rigorous and deeply concerned about wrongful convictions. She has seen too many cases where juries convicted on the strength of a single eyewitness without considering base rates.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Ninety-nine percent accurate sounds like a slam dunk. But I have learned that the most dangerous number in a courtroom is the one everyone assumes they understand. Do the math before you send someone to the dungeon.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correct reasoning earns the player a 'Bayesian Lens' — an in-game tool that reveals base rates and helps compute posterior probabilities in future evidence-evaluation quests.

scenario.context: The player visits the town physician in Millhaven, who has just received the results of a medical screening test. A patient has tested positive for a rare disease, and the physician wants the player to help compute the actual probability of illness.
scenario.text: The physician says: 'A patient just tested positive for colon blight. The test is 95% accurate — it correctly identifies 95% of people who have the disease (sensitivity), and correctly clears 95% of people who do not have the disease (specificity). The patient is terrified and believes there is a 95% chance she has colon blight. But the base rate of colon blight is only 0.5% of the population. Help me compute the true probability so I can counsel her properly.'
scenario.speaker_context: This is directly from Bert's lecture notes on the base rate fallacy, using his colon cancer screening example. The patient commits the base rate fallacy by equating the test accuracy with the probability of disease given a positive result.

structure.pattern_name: Base rate reasoning in medical screening
structure.pattern_description: For a population of 100,000: 500 have colon blight (0.5% base rate). Of those 500, the test correctly identifies 95% = 475 true positives. Of the 99,500 without the disease, the test incorrectly flags 5% = 4,975 false positives. Total positive results = 475 + 4,975 = 5,450. P(disease | positive test) = 475 / 5,450 = approximately 8.7%. The patient's actual risk is about 8.7%, not 95%. When the true condition is rare, even highly accurate tests produce many more false positives than true positives.
structure.formal_form: Base rate: P(D) = 0.005. Sensitivity: P(+|D) = 0.95. Specificity: P(-|~D) = 0.95, so P(+|~D) = 0.05. Population: 100,000. Diseased: 500. True positives: 475. Healthy: 99,500. False positives: 4,975. P(D|+) = 475/(475+4975) = 475/5450 ≈ 0.087 = 8.7%.
structure.why_right: The base rate fallacy occurs when people ignore the prior probability of a condition and treat the test accuracy as the probability of having the condition. When a disease is rare (0.5%), the 5% false positive rate applied to the large healthy population generates far more false positives than the 95% true positive rate generates from the small diseased population. The natural frequency approach (counting in a population of 100,000) makes this intuitive: 4,975 false alarms versus 475 real cases.
structure.counterpoint: A positive test result is not meaningless — it raised the probability from 0.5% to 8.7%, a 17-fold increase. The appropriate response is further testing, not panic and not dismissal. Multiple independent positive tests would continue to raise the probability.

assessment.identification_prompt: The patient believes she has a 95% chance of having colon blight. Is she right? Use the base rate and test accuracy to compute the actual probability. Show your work.

rubric.description: Player agrees with the patient that the probability is 95% or close to it.
Player recognizes the probability is lower than 95% but cannot compute or explain why.
Player attempts the calculation using natural frequencies but makes arithmetic errors.
Player correctly computes approximately 8.7% using natural frequencies and explains why the base rate matters.

Player does all the above, explains the base rate fallacy by name, notes that the positive test still increased the probability from 0.5% to 8.7%, and suggests further testing rather than either panic or dismissal.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Let us use concrete numbers. Imagine 100,000 people. How many actually have the disease? How many of those will the test correctly catch? Now, how many healthy people are there? How many of those will the test incorrectly flag? Compare those two numbers.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. The physician now asks: what if the disease were more common — say, 10% base rate instead of 0.5%? How would that change the calculation? And what does that tell you about when screening tests are most reliable?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The physician is compassionate and evidence-based. She has seen too many patients terrified by positive screening results and wants the player to help her explain the math in a way patients can understand.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The test says positive. The patient hears death sentence. But the numbers tell a different story. When the disease is rare, most positive results are false alarms. That is not intuition — it is arithmetic.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correct computation earns the player a 'Base Rate Calculator' — an in-game tool for evaluating screening and diagnostic evidence. The physician also offers a follow-up quest investigating whether a second independent test changes the probability.

scenario.context: The player enters the Ironvale town hall where the council is debating whether to allow a new bakery to open on Market Street. Councillor Varn, who owns the only existing bakery, stands to oppose the permit.
scenario.text: Councillor Varn rises, visibly agitated. 'If we allow a second bakery on Market Street, the competition will drive down bread prices. If prices drop, both bakeries will cut corners on ingredients. If they cut corners, people will get sick from bad flour. If people get sick, the healers' hall will be overwhelmed. If the healers are overwhelmed, a plague will sweep through Ironvale. Mark my words: approving this permit is the first step toward a plague that will empty this town.'
scenario.speaker_context: Councillor Varn owns the only bakery in Ironvale and has a financial interest in blocking competition. He presents a chain of causal claims, each plausible-sounding in isolation, but the cumulative probability of the entire chain is very low.

structure.pattern_description: Varn chains together a sequence of causal claims — competition leads to price drops leads to corner-cutting leads to illness leads to overwhelmed healers leads to plague — treating each link as inevitable. Even if each individual step had a 90% probability, the probability of the entire six-step chain would be roughly 0.9^5 = 0.59, and the actual probabilities are far lower than 90%.
structure.formal_form: A causes B. B causes C. C causes D. ... Therefore A causes Z. (But P(B|A) * P(C|B) * P(D|C) * ... is much less than any individual conditional probability.)
structure.why_wrong: Probabilities are not preserved across a chain of causal claims. Each link in the chain has its own probability of occurring, and the joint probability of the entire sequence is the product of all the individual probabilities, which shrinks rapidly. Varn treats each step as certain when none of them are. Contrast this with hypothetical syllogism, which preserves validity because it deals with logical necessity, not probability.
structure.counterpoint: If each causal link were genuinely near-certain (backed by evidence), then concern about the chain would be warranted. The fallacy lies in asserting a long causal chain without establishing that each link is highly probable.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councillor Varn seems very worried about this bakery permit. He has given you a chain of consequences. Do you find his reasoning convincing? Why or why not?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Varn or sees nothing wrong with the chain of reasoning.
Player feels the conclusion is too extreme but cannot explain why the reasoning fails.
Player notices that the chain seems unlikely but does not articulate the probability issue.
Player identifies that each step in the chain is uncertain and that stringing uncertain steps together makes the final outcome very unlikely.
Player identifies the causal slippery slope, explains that probabilities multiply across the chain and therefore diminish rapidly, and can distinguish this from valid hypothetical syllogism.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Let's take Varn's chain one step at a time. Is it certain that a second bakery would drive down prices? Even if it did, is it certain that both bakeries would cut corners? Assign a rough probability to each step, then multiply them together. What happens?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider: Varn's chain looks a lot like hypothetical syllogism (if A then B, if B then C, therefore if A then C). Why does hypothetical syllogism work in deductive logic but this chain does not work in causal reasoning?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Councillor Varn is a nervous, self-interested baker who genuinely believes his own catastrophizing. He speaks rapidly, building momentum with each link in the chain, and grows more alarmed as he goes.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think it is just a bakery? That is how it starts. Just a bakery. Then the prices fall. Then the flour goes bad. Then the sickness comes. I have seen it before — well, not exactly, but I can see it coming.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy and explains the probability issue, the council votes to approve the permit. Varn grudgingly admits he was mainly worried about competition. The new baker offers the player a discount and a side quest involving supply chain logistics.

scenario.context: The player visits the Arcane Academy in Thornwall, where students are studying the nature of matter. In a courtyard lecture, a first-year student named Pip is trying to impress his classmates with a philosophical argument about visibility.
scenario.text: Pip stands on a bench and announces proudly: 'I have proven that I am invisible! Listen carefully. Every atom in my body is invisible to the naked eye. I am made entirely of atoms. Therefore, I must be invisible to the naked eye!' He waves his arms. 'You only think you can see me because of habit!'
scenario.speaker_context: Pip is a first-year student at the Arcane Academy, eager to show off logical reasoning he half-learned in class. He is applying a property of the parts to the whole without considering whether the property transfers.

structure.pattern_description: Pip infers that a property true of each individual part (each atom is invisible) must be true of the whole composed of those parts (Pip is invisible). But visibility is not a property that transfers from parts to whole in this way — the arrangement and quantity of atoms creates emergent properties like visibility.
structure.formal_form: Each part of X has property P. Therefore X has property P. (Invalid when P does not transfer from parts to whole.)
structure.why_wrong: Properties of individual parts do not necessarily hold for the whole they compose. Each atom is invisible, but billions of atoms arranged into a human body are very much visible. Whether a property transfers from parts to whole depends on the specific property and the relationship between parts and whole — this requires domain knowledge, making composition an informal fallacy.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes the composition inference is valid. If every part of a statue is made of bronze, then the statue is made of bronze. The key is whether the property in question is the kind that aggregates. Visibility does not; material composition does.

assessment.identification_prompt: Pip seems very confident in his proof. Is his reasoning valid? Can you spot the mistake?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Pip or cannot identify a problem.
Player knows the conclusion is absurd but cannot explain the logical error.
Player recognizes that what is true of atoms is not necessarily true of a person, but cannot generalize the principle.
Player identifies that Pip is wrongly applying a property of the parts to the whole and can explain why visibility does not transfer this way.

Player identifies the composition fallacy, explains why the property does not transfer, and can give an example where the inference from parts to whole would be legitimate (e.g., material composition).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: each brick in a wall weighs two kilograms. Does the wall weigh two kilograms? Some properties of parts carry over to the whole and some do not. Which kind is visibility?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Nice. Now try this: every player on the team is excellent. Therefore the team is excellent. Is that composition, or is it legitimate? What would you need to know to decide?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pip is an enthusiastic, slightly obnoxious first-year student who loves showing off half-understood logic. He is not malicious, just overconfident. He gestures dramatically and speaks with theatrical flair.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Pip spots you and rushes over. 'You there! Traveler! Can you see me? Of course you think you can. But I have logically proven that you cannot. Let me explain...'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy, Pip is crestfallen but then excited to learn the correct principle. He becomes a recurring NPC who brings the player new 'proofs' to evaluate, unlocking a chain of informal fallacy puzzles.

scenario.context: The player is helping settle a property dispute in the village of Glenbrook. Old Harmon has died and left his house to his three children equally. The house has been appraised at 900 gold. The eldest son, Dorin, is arguing with the local assessor about the value of individual components.
scenario.text: Dorin slams the appraisal document on the table. 'This house is worth 900 gold. Therefore each beam, each stone, each nail in this house is worth its share of 900 gold. I want to sell just the oak beams from the attic — there are nine of them, and the house has about 900 components, so each beam is worth one gold. Wait, that cannot be right either. Look, the point is: the house costs 900 gold, so each part must carry that value proportionally!'
scenario.speaker_context: Dorin is trying to sell individual components of the house at prices derived from the total value. He assumes the value of the whole distributes to each part, ignoring that the house's value comes from the assembled structure, not the raw materials.

structure.pattern_description: Dorin infers that because the whole house has a certain property (being worth 900 gold), each part of the house must share that property proportionally. But the house's value comes from the arrangement and integration of its parts, not from the parts individually. Disassembled lumber and stones are worth far less than an assembled house.
structure.formal_form: X has property P. Y is a part of X. Therefore Y has property P (proportionally). (Invalid when P does not distribute from whole to parts.)
structure.why_wrong: The value of the house is an emergent property of its assembled structure — location, craftsmanship, functional integration. Individual beams and stones do not carry proportional shares of that value. A pile of disassembled building materials is worth a fraction of the intact house.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes properties do distribute from whole to parts. If the whole team died in an accident, then each individual member died. The fallacy occurs only when the property in question is emergent and does not transfer to individual components.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dorin is trying to figure out how much individual parts of the house are worth based on the total value. Does his reasoning work?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Dorin's reasoning or cannot identify a problem.
Player senses the conclusion is wrong but cannot explain why.
Player recognizes that parts are not worth what the whole is worth but cannot articulate the general principle.
Player identifies that Dorin wrongly applies a property of the whole to its parts and explains why value does not distribute this way.
Player names the division fallacy, explains emergent properties, and can provide examples where whole-to-part inference is legitimate versus illegitimate.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Suppose you disassemble the house entirely and lay every stone, beam, and nail in a pile. Would someone pay 900 gold for that pile? If not, where did the value go?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider Bert's trickier example: the team played their worst game. Therefore each individual player played their worst game. Is that division? Why is it harder to tell?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dorin is a frustrated, impatient eldest son who wants to extract maximum value from his inheritance. He is not dishonest, just reasoning poorly under pressure. He speaks in rapid, exasperated bursts.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Dorin corners you near the assessor's office. 'You look like someone with sense. Tell this fool that if the house is worth 900 gold, the parts must add up to 900 gold. That is just arithmetic!'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy, the assessor thanks them and Dorin grudgingly accepts that he needs to sell the house intact or accept a lower price for materials. The assessor offers the player a side quest evaluating other property claims in the village.

scenario.context: The player encounters a riddling trickster named Silvertongue at a crossroads. Silvertongue claims to have proven a paradoxical conclusion and bets the player five gold that they cannot find the flaw.
scenario.text: Silvertongue grins and recites: 'Nobody is perfect. Bert is a nobody. Therefore, Bert is perfect.' He pauses for effect. 'Logically airtight, wouldn't you say? The premises are true, the conclusion follows. Poor Bert — or perhaps lucky Bert!'
scenario.speaker_context: Silvertongue is a wandering trickster who uses equivocation puzzles to win bets. He knows the argument is fallacious but presents it as valid to test travelers. The word 'nobody' shifts meaning between the two premises: in the first it means 'no person,' in the second it means 'an unimportant person.'

structure.pattern_description: The argument uses the word 'nobody' in two different senses. In 'Nobody is perfect,' 'nobody' means 'no person' (a universal negative quantifier). In 'Bert is a nobody,' 'nobody' means 'an unimportant or insignificant person.' The argument treats these as the same meaning, creating an illusion of validity.
structure.formal_form: Term T is used with meaning M1 in premise 1. Term T is used with meaning M2 in premise 2. The conclusion follows only if T has the same meaning in both premises. Since M1 ≠ M2, the argument is invalid.
structure.why_wrong: The argument trades on an ambiguity. 'Nobody' as a quantifier (no person) and 'nobody' as a noun (an insignificant person) are different concepts. Once you disambiguate the two meanings, the argument clearly does not follow: 'No person is perfect' and 'Bert is an insignificant person' do not entail 'Bert is perfect.'
structure.counterpoint: This is Bert's favorite example from PHIL 201. A subtler form involves words like 'law' (laws of nature vs. laws of society) where the equivocation is harder to spot because the meanings are closer together.

assessment.identification_prompt: Silvertongue claims this argument is logically airtight. Is it? Where does the reasoning go wrong?

rubric.description: Player accepts the argument or cannot find a flaw.
Player feels something is wrong but cannot pinpoint the issue.
Player notices the word 'nobody' seems to mean different things but cannot fully articulate the problem.
Player identifies that 'nobody' has two meanings and that the argument only works if you conflate them.
Player identifies equivocation, explains both meanings precisely (quantifier vs. noun), and can provide another example of equivocation with a different ambiguous term.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Read the two premises slowly. In the first one, does 'nobody' refer to a specific person? In the second one, does it? Are these the same use of the word?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well spotted. Now try a harder one: 'The laws of biology are not made by any legislature. What is not made by a legislature is not a real law. Therefore the laws of biology are not real laws.' Same trick?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Silvertongue is a charming, theatrical trickster who delights in wordplay and logical puzzles. He is not malicious — he genuinely enjoys testing people's reasoning and pays up cheerfully when bested.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Silvertongue blocks your path with a flourish. 'A wager, traveler! Five gold says you cannot find the flaw in my perfect proof. And I do mean perfect.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the equivocation, Silvertongue pays the five gold and offers a harder puzzle (a subtler equivocation using 'law' or 'right'). He becomes a recurring NPC who guards crossroads with logic puzzles.

scenario.context: The player visits the Mages' Guild, where two scholars are debating the classification of magical abilities. Scholar Tilde argues that there is no real difference between a novice mage and an archmage.
scenario.text: Scholar Tilde gestures at a line of students practicing spells of increasing difficulty. 'Look at them. Can you tell me exactly where a novice becomes an apprentice? Where an apprentice becomes a journeyman? Where a journeyman becomes a master? You cannot draw a sharp line anywhere. Each student differs from the next by the tiniest increment of skill. Therefore, there is no real difference between a first-day novice who can barely light a candle and Archmage Velorin who can level a fortress. The ranks are arbitrary nonsense.'
scenario.speaker_context: Scholar Tilde is a skeptical academic who uses the absence of sharp boundaries to deny real differences. She is applying sorites-style reasoning: because there is no precise point where one category ends and another begins, she concludes the categories are meaningless.

structure.pattern_description: Tilde exploits the vagueness of category boundaries. Because there is no sharp line between novice and apprentice, or apprentice and journeyman, she concludes there is no real difference between the extremes. This is the sorites paradox applied to conceptual categories: if removing one grain of sand from a heap does not make it not-a-heap, then no amount of removal does, so there are no heaps.
structure.formal_form: There is no sharp boundary between A and B. There is no sharp boundary between B and C. ... Therefore there is no real difference between A and Z.
structure.why_wrong: The inability to draw a sharp boundary between adjacent cases does not mean there is no difference between the extremes. A first-day novice and an archmage differ enormously in ability, even if the transition between them is gradual. Vagueness in boundaries does not eliminate the reality of the categories at the extremes.
structure.counterpoint: Tilde's argument would prove too much: by the same logic, there is no difference between hot and cold (since temperature is a continuum), or between day and night (since twilight is gradual). The existence of borderline cases does not destroy clear cases.

assessment.identification_prompt: Scholar Tilde claims there is no real difference between a novice and an archmage because you cannot draw a sharp line between the ranks. Is she right?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Tilde that the ranks are meaningless.
Player disagrees but cannot articulate why vague boundaries do not eliminate real differences.
Player recognizes that the extremes are clearly different but struggles to explain why the lack of sharp boundaries does not matter.
Player identifies that Tilde confuses the absence of a sharp boundary with the absence of any difference, and notes that the extremes are clearly distinguishable.

Player identifies the conceptual slippery slope (sorites-style reasoning), explains that vagueness in boundaries does not eliminate differences at the extremes, and can provide an analogous example (e.g., bald/not-bald, heap/not-heap).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider temperature. You cannot point to the exact degree where 'warm' becomes 'hot.' Does that mean there is no difference between a summer day and a blast furnace?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider: does this mean all category boundaries are legitimate? Could someone use this same defense to justify an arbitrary distinction that really is meaningless? How would you tell the difference?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Scholar Tilde is a sharp-minded contrarian who enjoys using philosophical arguments to challenge institutional structures. She is intellectually honest but takes her skepticism too far.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Tilde intercepts you near the rank examination board. 'Novice, apprentice, journeyman, master, archmage — five words for one continuous spectrum. Show me where one ends and the next begins. You cannot, because the lines do not exist.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy, Tilde is impressed and concedes that the extremes are genuinely different even if the boundaries are fuzzy. She offers the player a puzzle about constructing fair category boundaries, unlocking a side quest about reforming the Guild's ranking system.

scenario.context: The player is investigating the background of a suspicious merchant named Linda who has arrived in the trading town of Portmere. The town guard captain asks the player to assess which profile is more likely based on what they know about Linda.
scenario.text: Guard Captain Hask slides a dossier across the table. 'Here is what we know about this Linda. She studied philosophy at the University of Thornwall. As a student, she was deeply involved in campaigns against unfair trade tariffs and participated in protests for merchant guild reform. She was outspoken and bright.' Hask leans back. 'Now, my deputy says it is more likely that Linda is a bank clerk AND a member of the Fair Trade Alliance than that she is simply a bank clerk. He says the activist profile just fits too well. I want your opinion — is my deputy's reasoning sound?'
scenario.speaker_context: Guard Captain Hask is testing the player's probabilistic reasoning. His deputy has fallen for the conjunction fallacy — judging a conjunction (bank clerk AND activist) as more probable than one of its conjuncts (bank clerk) because the conjunction fits a narrative better.

structure.pattern_description: The deputy judges P(bank clerk AND activist) > P(bank clerk). This violates a basic law of probability: the probability of a conjunction can never exceed the probability of either conjunct alone. P(A and B) <= P(A). The error occurs because the conjunction fits a compelling narrative (the 'representativeness heuristic'), making it feel more probable.
structure.formal_form: P(A and B) > P(A) is asserted. But by the conjunction rule, P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B|A) <= P(A). The conjunction can never be more probable than either individual component.
structure.why_wrong: A conjunction adds a constraint. Every bank clerk who is also an activist is already counted among the bank clerks. The set of people who are both A and B is a subset of the set of people who are A. No matter how well the activist profile fits Linda's background, adding that condition cannot make the description more probable — it can only make it equal or less probable.
structure.counterpoint: The deputy's intuition is not crazy — the conjunction is more 'representative' of Linda's description. The error is confusing representativeness (how well something fits a story) with probability (how likely it is). Kahneman and Tversky's original Linda problem demonstrates this systematically.

assessment.identification_prompt: The deputy thinks it is more likely that Linda is a bank clerk AND an activist than that she is just a bank clerk. Is the deputy's reasoning correct?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the deputy that the conjunction is more likely.
Player is unsure but cannot articulate the probability principle at stake.
Player recognizes something is wrong with comparing the two but cannot state the conjunction rule.
Player identifies that a conjunction cannot be more probable than either conjunct and explains why.

Player identifies the conjunction fallacy, states the probability rule P(A and B) <= P(A), explains the role of the representativeness heuristic in making the conjunction feel more likely, and can connect this to the original Linda problem.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about it this way: the set of all bank clerks includes bank clerks who are activists and bank clerks who are not activists. Can a subset ever be larger than the set that contains it?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now, why do you think people so reliably fall for this? What is it about the conjunction that makes it feel more probable even when it cannot be? This connects to the representativeness heuristic.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Guard Captain Hask is a methodical, no-nonsense investigator who tests recruits with reasoning puzzles before trusting them with real cases. He is gruff but fair, and visibly pleased when someone gets the answer right.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Hask pushes the file toward you. 'My deputy is a good man but sometimes he lets a good story override good logic. Tell me if he has done it again.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the fallacy, Hask promotes them to investigative consultant and gives them a more complex probabilistic reasoning challenge involving base rates (leading into A8.2).

scenario.context: The player is visiting the healers' hall in Thornwall. A healer named Sera has just received the results of a new diagnostic test for Stoneblight, a rare disease that affects 0.5% of the population. The test is 95% accurate — it correctly identifies 95% of people who have the disease (sensitivity) and correctly clears 95% of people who do not (specificity). A patient has just tested positive.
scenario.text: Sera looks at the test result and turns pale. 'The test came back positive for Stoneblight. The test is 95% accurate. So there is a 95% chance this patient has Stoneblight. We need to begin the expensive and painful treatment regimen immediately.' She begins preparing the reagents. 'I know the treatment is harsh, but with a 95% chance of infection, we cannot afford to wait.'
scenario.speaker_context: Sera is a competent healer who has confused the accuracy of the test with the probability that the patient actually has the disease. She is neglecting the base rate: Stoneblight is very rare (0.5%), so even a highly accurate test will produce many more false positives than true positives.

structure.pattern_description: Sera assumes that a positive result on a 95% accurate test means a 95% chance of disease. She ignores the base rate of 0.5%. For 100,000 people: 500 have Stoneblight. The test catches 475 of them (true positives). Of the 99,500 healthy people, the test falsely flags 5% = 4,975 (false positives). Total positives: 475 + 4,975 = 5,450. Probability of actually having Stoneblight given a positive test: 475/5,450 = 8.7%.
structure.why_wrong: When the base rate of a condition is very low, even a highly accurate test produces far more false positives than true positives. The 95% accuracy tells you about the test's performance, not about this patient's probability of being sick. Ignoring the base rate inflates the perceived probability from the actual 8.7% to a mistaken 95%.
structure.counterpoint: If the base rate were higher — say 50% — then a 95% accurate positive test would indeed indicate very high probability of disease. The base rate is not always negligible; the fallacy lies in ignoring it, not in always distrusting test results.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sera says there is a 95% chance the patient has Stoneblight based on the positive test. Is she right? What is the actual probability?

rubric.description: Player agrees that the probability is 95%.
Player suspects the probability is lower but cannot explain why.
Player mentions that the disease is rare and this should matter, but cannot compute the actual probability.
Player identifies base rate neglect, explains that the low prevalence creates many false positives, and arrives at approximately the correct probability (around 8-9%).

Player identifies base rate neglect, works through the calculation with true positives and false positives (or applies Bayes' theorem), arrives at ~8.7%, and can explain when the base rate matters more or less.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine 100,000 people take this test. How many actually have Stoneblight? Of those, how many will test positive? Now, of the healthy people, how many will falsely test positive? Compare the two numbers.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider: a guard says he is 99% accurate at identifying thieves and he has identified Nancy as a thief. In a crowd of 1,000 people where 5 are thieves, what is the probability Nancy is actually a thief?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Sera is a dedicated, slightly anxious healer who cares deeply about her patients. She is not foolish — she simply has not thought through the probabilistic implications. She responds well to clear numerical explanations.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Sera grabs your arm as you enter the healers' hall. 'Thank the gods you are here. I need a second opinion. The test says positive, 95% accurate. That means 95% chance of Stoneblight, yes? Should I start treatment?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player walks Sera through the base rate calculation, she is shocked and grateful. She delays treatment and orders a second test. She then asks the player to help her understand false positives better, unlocking a probability workshop side quest.

scenario.context: The player arrives in the kingdom's capital where the Royal Education Ministry is presenting findings about school performance. Minister Kael is announcing a major new initiative based on a study of school achievement scores across the realm.
scenario.text: Minister Kael unrolls a large chart before the assembled officials. 'We have studied every school in the realm. The results are clear: the highest-performing schools are overwhelmingly small village schools with fewer than thirty students. Oakhollow, with twelve students, topped the rankings. Millpond, with eighteen, came second. The evidence proves that small schools produce better scholars. I am therefore allocating 1.7 million gold to split our large city schools into smaller academies. Smaller is better — the data does not lie.'
scenario.speaker_context: Minister Kael has observed a real pattern — small schools do top the rankings — but has committed the small numbers fallacy by seeking a causal explanation for what is actually a statistical artifact. Smaller samples produce more extreme results in both directions.

structure.pattern_name: Law of small numbers / small numbers fallacy
structure.pattern_description: Kael observes that small schools top the achievement rankings and concludes that being small causes better performance. But smaller populations produce more variable outcomes: with fewer students, a few strong (or weak) performers swing the average dramatically. If Kael checked the bottom of the rankings, he would find small schools there too. This is a mathematical property of small samples, not a causal property of school size.
structure.formal_form: Small groups show extreme outcomes (both high and low). Observer notices extreme outcomes at one end. Observer infers a causal explanation for the extremity. But the explanation is statistical: small sample variance, not a causal factor.
structure.why_wrong: The law of small numbers states that smaller groups will tend to inhabit the extremes of any ranking. Kael only checked the top — if he checked the bottom, he would also find small schools. The pattern is an artifact of sample size variance, not evidence that small schools are better. The Gates Foundation made exactly this mistake, spending $1.7 billion before realizing that small schools also dominated the bottom of the rankings.
structure.counterpoint: Small schools may genuinely have some advantages (e.g., more individual attention). The fallacy is not in considering the hypothesis but in treating the ranking data as sufficient evidence. A proper study would compare average performance across school sizes, not just look at extremes.

assessment.identification_prompt: Minister Kael says the data proves small schools produce better scholars. Is the data as convincing as he thinks? What should he check before spending 1.7 million gold?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Kael that small schools are better and the investment is justified.
Player is skeptical but cannot explain why small schools might top the rankings without being genuinely better.
Player suggests checking more data but does not identify the specific statistical issue with small samples.
Player identifies that small samples produce extreme results and suggests checking the bottom of the rankings for small schools too.

Player explains the law of small numbers, predicts small schools at the bottom of the rankings, explains that this is a mathematical artifact of sample size rather than a causal factor, and suggests a more appropriate study design.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Before you agree with Kael, answer this: what do you think you would find at the very bottom of the rankings? Would you find large schools or small ones?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. The Gates Foundation actually made this exact mistake and spent $1.7 billion on it. How could Kael design a study that would actually tell him whether school size matters, as opposed to just reflecting sample size effects?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Minister Kael is a well-meaning bureaucrat who loves data but lacks statistical training. He is proud of his study and defensive when challenged, but honest enough to reconsider when shown a clear error.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Kael beams at the chart. 'The numbers speak for themselves! Oakhollow, twelve students, top of the realm! You cannot argue with data, friend.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player explains the law of small numbers and suggests checking the bottom of the rankings, Kael sends an aide to compile the data. The aide returns confirming that small schools are overrepresented at the bottom too. Kael grudgingly delays the initiative and hires the player as a statistical consultant.

scenario.context: The player visits a village market where a traveling peddler named Quick Salve Sal is advertising a miraculous cold remedy. A crowd has gathered and several satisfied customers are testifying.
scenario.text: Sal holds up a small vial of greenish liquid. 'Three days ago, Farmer Gerd here was sneezing, coughing, miserable with the worst cold of the season. He took one dose of Sal's Supreme Elixir. And today? Fit as a fiddle! Tell them, Gerd!' Gerd nods enthusiastically. 'It is true. I was dying, and now I am well.' Sal turns to the crowd. 'Nine out of ten of my customers report feeling better within three days of taking the elixir. Nine out of ten! Can any other remedy claim that?'
scenario.speaker_context: Sal is exploiting the natural course of illness. People buy cold remedies when they feel their worst — which is also when they are most likely to improve naturally. Regression to the mean ensures that most customers would have gotten better anyway, with or without the elixir.

structure.pattern_description: People seek remedies when symptoms are at their peak (an extreme observation). After peak symptoms, the natural tendency is to return to baseline health — this is regression to the mean. Sal attributes the improvement to his elixir, but the improvement would likely have occurred regardless. The nine-out-of-ten success rate reflects the natural recovery rate from colds, not the efficacy of the treatment.
structure.formal_form: Extreme observation X occurs (peak illness). Intervention I is applied. Observation returns toward the mean (natural recovery). Causal credit is given to I, when regression to the mean is the more parsimonious explanation.
structure.why_wrong: Colds typically last a few days and resolve on their own. People buy remedies when they feel worst, which is exactly when improvement is most likely regardless of treatment. To show the elixir actually works, you would need a comparison group: people who were equally sick but did not take the elixir. If both groups recover at the same rate, the elixir does nothing.
structure.counterpoint: Not every post-peak improvement is regression to the mean. Some treatments genuinely work. The point is that recovery after peak symptoms is not itself evidence of efficacy — you need a controlled comparison to distinguish real effects from regression.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sal says nine out of ten customers feel better after taking his elixir. Is this good evidence that the elixir works?

rubric.description: Player is convinced by the testimonials and the nine-out-of-ten figure.
Player is skeptical but cannot explain why the testimonials are unreliable.
Player suggests the customers might have gotten better on their own but cannot name the statistical phenomenon.
Player identifies regression to the mean: people buy the remedy at peak illness, and natural recovery is the most likely explanation for improvement.

Player identifies regression to the mean, explains why testimonials at peak illness are unreliable evidence, and describes what a proper controlled test would look like (treatment vs. control group comparison).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about when people buy cold remedies. Is it at the beginning of a cold, the middle, or the worst point? And what usually happens to a cold after its worst point, with or without medicine?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider: a sports commentator says a player who had a record-breaking season last year is 'slumping' this year because they changed their training routine. Could regression to the mean explain the 'slump' instead?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Quick Salve Sal is a cheerful, fast-talking peddler who may or may not believe in his own product. He is charming, uses testimonials aggressively, and deflects criticism with humor.
