Yorn likes Ella, so he interprets ambiguous evidence in her favor. He distrusts Rusk, so he interprets identical evidence against him. The evidence has not changed — the lens through which it is evaluated has.
structure.formal_form: Agent forms positive impression I+ of person P1. Agent forms negative impression I- of person P2. Identical evidence E is evaluated: E|I+ is interpreted charitably; E|I- is interpreted harshly. The evaluation is driven by I, not E.
structure.why_wrong: The halo effect undermines fair evaluation by allowing an overall impression to contaminate specific judgments. In a courtroom, it means likeable defendants are acquitted and unlikeable defendants are convicted on the same evidence. The same pattern distorts hiring, grading, reviews, and any context where a general impression affects specific assessments.
structure.counterpoint: First impressions are not always irrelevant. Character evidence can be legitimately probative in some contexts. The error is in letting a general feeling override careful evaluation of specific evidence, especially when the stakes are high and fairness demands equal treatment.

assessment.identification_prompt: Magistrate Yorn acquitted Ella and convicted Rusk on identical evidence. What is different between the two cases, and how is it affecting his judgment?

rubric.description: Player accepts the verdicts and believes the evidence must be different for each case or that character justifies the distinction.
Player notices the verdicts are inconsistent but attributes it to simple personal dislike rather than a cognitive pattern.
Player recognizes that Yorn likes Ella and dislikes Rusk, and that this is influencing his interpretation of the evidence, but does not name the halo effect.

Player identifies the halo effect: Yorn's positive impression of Ella causes charitable interpretation of evidence, while his negative impression of Rusk causes harsh interpretation of the same evidence.

Player identifies the halo effect, explains how it distorts evaluation of specific evidence, connects it to systemic injustice, and proposes structural safeguards (blind review of evidence, standardized evaluation criteria).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Cover up the names and read just the evidence for each case. Grain dust. Near the granary. No alibi. Can you tell which suspect is which from the evidence alone? If not, why did Yorn reach different conclusions?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The halo effect does not just operate in courtrooms. Think about job interviews, student evaluations, or product reviews. How does liking someone change how you evaluate their work? What structures can prevent this?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Magistrate Yorn is not corrupt — he is genuinely unaware that his liking for Ella and distrust of Rusk are coloring his evaluation. He considers himself scrupulously fair. The court clerk is observant and troubled but does not have the authority to intervene.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The court clerk pulls you aside. 'Did you notice what just happened? Same evidence, opposite verdicts. I've seen Yorn do this before — the people he likes always seem to have weaker evidence against them. He doesn't see it.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the halo effect, the court clerk asks them to present the argument to the appeals council. The player presents the evidence side by side, stripped of personal details. The council overturns Rusk's conviction and orders a fair retrial for both. Yorn is initially defensive but later acknowledges the pattern. The player earns a role as a court advisor.

scenario.context: The player is walking through a crowded market square in the city of Coppergate when they witness a pickpocket steal a merchant's purse in broad daylight. At least twenty people saw it happen. The merchant shouts for help. Nobody moves.
scenario.text: The merchant stumbles and shouts: 'Thief! He took my purse! Someone stop him!' The player looks around. Twenty people stand frozen. A baker watches from his stall. A guard leans against a wall, looking at the crowd, apparently waiting for someone else to act. A woman clutches her child and steps back. The thief jogs unhurriedly toward the alley, not even running. He knows no one will act. The baker mutters to his apprentice: 'Someone will get him.' The guard thinks: 'Not my patrol sector.' The woman thinks: 'Surely someone closer will help.' Nobody moves.
scenario.speaker_context: Every bystander has a reason not to act, and that reason is the same: the presence of other bystanders. Each person assumes someone else will intervene, and this assumption is shared by everyone, resulting in collective inaction.

structure.pattern_description: The bystander effect occurs when the presence of others reduces each individual's sense of personal responsibility to act. In a crowd, each person assumes someone else will intervene (diffusion of responsibility), looks to others' inaction as a signal that action is not needed (pluralistic ignorance), and fears embarrassment from acting in a situation others seem to deem non-urgent (evaluation apprehension). The result: the more witnesses, the less likely any single person is to help.
structure.formal_form: N bystanders witness emergency E. Each bystander i estimates P(someone else acts) as high because N is large. Each bystander i's probability of acting, P(i acts), decreases as N increases. If all reason identically, P(anyone acts) approaches zero as N grows.
structure.why_wrong: The bystander effect turns numbers — which should increase the chance of help — into a liability. Each additional witness reduces rather than increases the probability of intervention because responsibility is diffused across more people. The victim is worse off in a crowd than with a single witness.
structure.counterpoint: The bystander effect is not inevitable. Research shows that assigning specific responsibility ('You in the red shirt, call for help') breaks the diffusion. Training and cultural norms also mitigate the effect. The pattern describes a default, not an unbreakable law.

assessment.identification_prompt: Twenty people watched the theft and nobody acted. Each person had a reason — but it was the same reason. What is it, and why does having more witnesses make help less likely rather than more likely?

rubric.description: Player attributes the inaction to cowardice or apathy without identifying the structural mechanism.
Player recognizes people are waiting for someone else but does not explain why this paralysis increases with crowd size.
Player identifies diffusion of responsibility but does not connect it to pluralistic ignorance or evaluation apprehension.
Player identifies the bystander effect, explains diffusion of responsibility, and recognizes that each person's inaction reinforces the others'.

Player identifies the bystander effect with all three mechanisms (diffusion, pluralistic ignorance, evaluation apprehension), explains the paradox of crowd size, and can describe how to break the effect.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine you were the only person in the square when the theft happened. Would you have acted? Now imagine twenty people around you, all standing still. Does their stillness change your impulse to help? Why?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the practical lesson: if you ever need help in a crowd, do not shout 'someone help!' Instead, point to one specific person and say 'You, in the blue coat — call the guard.' Why does this work?

game_hooks.npc_personality: The baker is a decent person who genuinely assumed someone closer would act. The guard is bureaucratic and jurisdiction-minded. The thief is casual and experienced — he knows crowds are his best cover. The merchant is desperate and confused by the inaction.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The merchant sits in the dirt, stunned. 'Twenty people. Twenty people watched. I looked right at the guard and he looked right back at me and did nothing. Is everyone in this city a coward?' The baker overhears and looks ashamed. 'I'm not a coward. I just thought... someone else...'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the bystander effect, the merchant asks how to prevent it in the future. The player helps establish a 'market watch' system where specific stall owners are assigned specific response roles, eliminating diffusion of responsibility. Theft in the market drops dramatically. The player earns the merchant's gratitude and a discount at all Coppergate shops.
